title: Many-body Entanglement Quantification In Arbitrary States Through A Few Partial-transpose Moments
authors: A. S. Majumdar Sudip Chakrabarty
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can the entanglement of an arbitrary many-body state be quantified without reconstructing the state? We answer the question affirmatively by showing how the measure of logarithmic negativity can be estimated using a finite number of even partial transpose (PT) moments of a many-body state. Considering the squared PT spectrum as a probability measure, we solve exactly the task of a truncated Hausdorff moment problem with Gauss and Gauss-Radau quadrature. We obtain a hierarchy of lower bounds on the logarithmic negativity, which improves with increasing order of moments. Convergence to the exact value of the measure can be achieved for every state of finite dimension. We illustrate the bounds for ground states of three different interacting spin models, as well as for a thermal state. An error analysis demonstrates the efficacy of our scheme towards handling the limitation of finite statistics encountered in actual experiments with randomized measurements. Moreover, an example of density matrix renormalization group based numerical estimation is provided for handling system sizes beyond the scope of exact diagonalization.
tldr: The paper shows that the logarithmic negativity of an arbitrary many-body state can be estimated from a finite number of even partial-transpose moments by solving a truncated Hausdorff moment problem via Gauss and Gauss-Radau quadrature, yielding a converging hierarchy of lower bounds.
motivation: Full state tomography is prohibitive for many-body systems, so there is a strong need for entanglement measures that can be estimated directly from experimentally accessible data such as randomized-measurement moments.
method: Treating the squared partial-transpose spectrum as a probability measure, the authors solve the truncated Hausdorff moment problem exactly with Gauss and Gauss-Radau quadrature to construct a hierarchy of lower bounds on logarithmic negativity, including an error analysis for finite statistics and a DMRG-based numerical scheme for large systems.
result: The hierarchy of bounds improves monotonically with the number of moments and converges to the exact logarithmic negativity for any finite-dimensional state; the approach is illustrated on ground states of three interacting spin models, a thermal state, and larger systems treated with DMRG.
conclusion: Partial-transpose moments provide a practical, tomographically inexpensive route to certified entanglement quantification in many-body experiments, with controllable convergence and robustness to finite sampling.

title: Probability Bounds On Trajectory-level Exceedances Of Quantum Speed Limits Under Continuous-measurement Feedback
authors: Kohei Kobayashi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the probability that a conditioned quantum trajectory exceeds an ensemble-derived quantum speed limit (QSL) velocity under continuous measurement-based feedback. Using the finite-time average fidelity velocity, we derive an upper bound on the exceedance probability in terms of its mean and variance. We further obtain state-independent bounds from uniform constraints on the fidelity drift and diffusion, including an exponential concentration bound. For a feedback-controlled qubit, we derive explicit model-specific bounds and show that they are nontrivial in a short-time regime. We also identify a finite-time regime in which the exceedance probability vanishes exactly due to the restricted support of the conditioned dynamics. Monte Carlo simulations confirm the analytical bounds and illustrate their tightness.
tldr: The paper derives probability bounds on when conditioned quantum trajectories exceed an ensemble-derived quantum speed limit velocity under continuous-measurement feedback.
motivation: Quantum speed limits usually constrain ensemble-averaged evolution, but individual measured trajectories can fluctuate; understanding and bounding such trajectory-level exceedances is important for feedback-controlled quantum protocols.
method: Using finite-time average fidelity velocity, the authors bound exceedance probabilities via mean-variance inequalities and obtain state-independent exponential concentration bounds from uniform fidelity drift and diffusion constraints, with explicit analysis for a feedback-controlled qubit.
result: The bounds are nontrivial at short times, can become exactly zero in a finite-time regime due to restricted conditioned dynamics, and are confirmed and shown to be reasonably tight by Monte Carlo simulations.
conclusion: Trajectory-level violations of ensemble quantum speed limits can be probabilistically controlled under continuous-measurement feedback, providing quantitative constraints relevant to thermodynamic/control bounds on quantum information processing.

title: Thermodynamic Characterization Of Message-passing: Framework And Initial Study
authors: Stark C. Draper Kalana G. Abeywardena
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the thermodynamic efficiency of message-passing decoders using the mismatch cost framework. This framework quantifies the excess entropy generated when a system operates away from the thermodynamically optimal initial distribution. It provides a computable lower bound on irrecoverable energy loss. The decoder is modeled as a main decoding program with local message updates implemented as subroutines. Memory is treated as an external copying subsystem whose thermodynamic cost is excluded. Studying the [MATH] Hamming code transmitted over a binary erasure channel, we show how the channel-induced initialization statistics and the step-wise evolution of the algorithmic state distribution during decoding determine the total mismatch cost. We further show that different thermodynamically optimal state distributions, representing different underlying physical implementations of the decoder, can produce different thermodynamic costs for identical decoding dynamics. Conditioning the input distribution on correctable and non-correctable erasure patterns further reveals distinct thermodynamic signatures. These results demonstrate that thermodynamic cost is jointly governed by decoding dynamics, input statistics, and hardware characteristics. This points to opportunities for thermodynamically-informed decoder design to realize energy-efficient physical implementations.
tldr: The paper develops a mismatch-cost framework to characterize the thermodynamic efficiency of message-passing decoders, illustrated for a Hamming code over a binary erasure channel.
motivation: Understanding the thermodynamic cost of computation is important for energy-efficient implementations, and message-passing decoders are a key class of algorithms whose irreversible information processing costs have not been thermodynamically characterized in detail.
method: The decoder is modeled as a main decoding program with local message updates as subroutines, and mismatch cost is used to quantify excess entropy generation away from thermodynamically optimal initial distributions; the analysis is applied to a Hamming code transmitted over a binary erasure channel.
result: The total mismatch cost is shown to depend on channel-induced initialization statistics, the step-wise evolution of the algorithmic state distribution, and the choice of thermodynamically optimal state distribution corresponding to different physical implementations; conditioning on correctable versus non-correctable erasure patterns reveals distinct thermodynamic signatures.
conclusion: Thermodynamic cost is jointly governed by decoding dynamics, input statistics, and hardware characteristics, suggesting opportunities for thermodynamically informed decoder design and energy-efficient physical implementations.

title: Coherent Optical Control Of A Single Donor Electron Spin
authors: Yuxi Jiang, Amirehsan Alizadehherfati, Christine Falter, Jasvith R. Basani, Nils von Den Driesch, Yurii Kutovyi, Jan Seelbinder, Alexander Pawlis, Edo Waks
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36423v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coherent spin-photon interfaces are essential for scalable quantum networks, but their realization requires optically bright transitions, long-lived spin coherence, and complete coherent control. Donor-bound electron spins in II-VI semiconductors offer an attractive platform for optically active spin qubits because they combine strong donor-bound exciton transitions in a direct-bandgap material with a potentially nuclear-spin-free environment. However, coherent control of an individual optically active donor spin has remained elusive. Here we demonstrate optical initialization, coherent control, and readout of a single donor-bound electron spin in ZnSe. Using spin-selective donor-bound exciton optical transitions, we initialize the electron spin and directly resolve its spin-relaxation dynamics. We achieve coherent spin control with off-resonant picosecond optical pulses, as demonstrated by spin Rabi oscillations and Ramsey interference. We further coherently drive two spin-selective optical transitions and observe high-contrast coherent population trapping, demonstrating the formation of an optically controlled dark state. At higher driving strengths, multiple dark resonances reveal the hyperfine interaction between the electron and the I = 3/2 Cl nucleus. These results establish the first coherent optical control of a single donor electron spin in a II-VI semiconductor and identify isolated optical donors as a promising platform for solid-state optically active qubits.
tldr: The paper demonstrates optical initialization, coherent control, and readout of a single donor-bound electron spin in ZnSe, establishing a II-VI semiconductor donor as an optically active spin qubit platform.
motivation: Coherent spin-photon interfaces are needed for scalable quantum networks, but individual optically active donor spins have lacked full coherent control. Donor-bound electrons in direct-bandgap II-VI semiconductors may combine bright optical transitions with long spin coherence.
method: Using spin-selective donor-bound exciton transitions in ZnSe, the authors initialize and read out a single electron spin, resolve spin relaxation, and drive spin Rabi oscillations and Ramsey interference with off-resonant picosecond pulses. They also drive two spin-selective transitions to observe coherent population trapping and hyperfine-induced dark resonances.
result: The work achieves coherent optical control of a single donor electron spin, including Rabi oscillations, Ramsey interference, high-contrast coherent population trapping, and signatures of hyperfine coupling to the I=3/2 Cl nucleus.
conclusion: This establishes the first coherent optical control of a single donor electron spin in a II-VI semiconductor and identifies isolated optical donors as a promising solid-state platform for optically active qubits and spin-photon interfaces.

title: Controlled Dark-State Energy Storage And Work Extraction In V-Type Quantum Batteries
authors: H. H. Jen Chia-Hung Chu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36704v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The performance of a quantum battery depends not only on its ability to retain stored energy against unwanted discharge but also on the amount of useful work that can be extracted from it. Here, we investigate these complementary aspects in an ensemble of V-type qutrits coupled to a lossy cavity. By applying a finite splitting pulse to the two excited states of each qutrit, cavity-bright excitations are converted into atomic dark states, whose populations remain protected upon restoring degeneracy, even while the light-matter coupling remains active. Simulations with finite-duration pulses reveal a capture window governed by the competition among energy transfer, bright-to-dark conversion, and photon leakage. We further show that if the energy is stored in the fully symmetric atomic subspace, the passive energy is bounded by twice the transition energy for number of atoms [MATH]. Consequently, if the stored energy scales extensively with [MATH], the ratio of extractable work to stored energy approaches unity in the thermodynamic limit. Comparing different initial preparations at equal mean input energy, we find that coherent-state can yield greater finite-time ergotropy despite capturing less energy, whereas Fock-state favors greater extractable work in the stationary component. Our results demonstrate how controlled dark-state population trapping in an atom-cavity coupled system can protect stored energy while providing a conditional route toward high extractable work.
tldr: The paper studies an ensemble of V-type qutrits in a lossy cavity for dark-state energy storage and work extraction in a quantum battery.
motivation: Quantum batteries must both retain stored energy against discharge and allow useful work extraction, motivating controlled storage schemes.
method: Finite splitting pulses convert cavity-bright excitations into atomic dark states, and simulations compare finite-duration pulse capture dynamics and different initial preparations.
result: Dark-state populations remain protected after restoring degeneracy; stored passive energy is bounded and extractable-work ratios approach unity in the thermodynamic limit, with coherent states giving larger finite-time ergotropy and Fock states favoring stationary extractable work.
conclusion: Controlled dark-state trapping can protect stored energy while providing a conditional route to high extractable work in atom-cavity quantum batteries.

These dark states are protected from cavity decay when the degeneracy is restored, even with light-matter coupling active. Through simulations with finite-duration pulses, they identify a capture window determined by the interplay of energy transfer, bright-to-dark conversion, and photon leakage. They further derive a bound on passive energy for the fully symmetric atomic subspace: for N≥2 atoms, the passive energy is at most twice the transition energy. title: Finite-temperature Quantum Quasinormal Mode Theory For Spatiotemporally-resolved Dissipative Cavity Quantum Magnonics
authors: Lars Meschede, Daniel D. A. Clarke, Ortwin Hess
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36385v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cavity quantum magnonics has ushered in an unprecedented era of hybrid light-matter interfaces in which microwave photons, collective spin excitations, and superconducting or spin qubits can be coupled within a single device architecture, facilitating a versatile platform for quantum information processing. Realizing their full potential, however, requires a theory that can treat non-reciprocal magnetic media, material dissipation and open-cavity radiation losses, as well as finite-temperature fluctuations rigorously and without significant approximation. The dissipative magnonic resonances of such systems are described as quasinormal modes (QNMs), yet a consistent quantization procedure for lossy gyrotropic resonators has remained elusive. In this work, we present a finite-temperature quantum QNM theory, based on macroscopic quantum electrodynamics for non-reciprocal media and complex coordinate transformations, that achieves QNM quantization for a wide class of spatially inhomogeneous, dissipative and dispersive, cavity magnonic systems. We demonstrate the predictive capabilities of our theory via applications to hybrid dielectric-magnonic resonators interacting with both spin and superconducting qubits, evidencing modal interference effects, a continuous transition from coherent to dissipative coupling, spatiotemporal quantum field dynamics, and magnon-mediated qubit synchronization, at both zero and finite temperatures. By addressing the intricacies of modal loss and non-reciprocity in a fully quantum theory of cavity magnonics, our approach enables the quantitative design of hybrid quantum devices that operate under realistic open-system and thermal conditions, without recourse to ad hoc quantization schemes.

conclusion: The framework provides a first-principles, quantitatively predictive tool for designing hybrid quantum magnonic devices operating under realistic open-system and thermal conditions.

title: Suppressing Microwave Crosstalk In Superconducting Quantum Processors By Designing Parasitic Drive Capacitances
authors: Anuj Aggarwal, Jorge Fern\'andez-Pend\'as, Simon Pettersson Fors, Zakaria Mohamed, Halld\'or Jakobsson, Amr Osman, Janka Bizn\'arov\'a, Andreas Nylander, Anita Fadavi Roudsari, Marcus Rommel, Anton Frisk Kockum, Giovanna Tancredi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36365v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As superconducting quantum processors scale to large qubit counts, unwanted microwave drive crosstalk becomes an important source of coherent errors. Here, we investigate the role of parasitic coupling paths in the suppression of drive crosstalk in a processor with two fixed-frequency transmon qubits and a tunable coupler. To account for the many different coupling paths, we develop a detailed circuit model to capture the dependence of crosstalk on the coupler frequency. We experimentally demonstrate suppression of crosstalk, finding that the suppression does not originate solely from cancellation of the effective qubit-qubit coupling, but also is a result of interference between other coupling paths. Building on these insights, we show that drive crosstalk can be suppressed with the right choice of parasitic capacitances, which otherwise often are treated as unwanted design imperfections. Our results provide practical guidance for low-crosstalk device design of superconducting quantum processors and point toward a broader strategy in which parasitic coupling paths are engineered rather than simply minimized.

title: Ancestor Lifting Of Quasi-Cyclic Additive Codes And Certified Quantum Codes
authors: Liangdong Lu, Ran Xu, Ruipan Yang, Qiang Fu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Additive codes over [MATH] that are self-orthogonal under the trace inner product correspond to binary quantum stabilizer codes. We study 1-generator [MATH]-quasi-cyclic (QC) additive codes and their exact quantum distances. For composite lengths [MATH], an ancestor-lifting theorem transports dual words of the folded ancestor to the length-[MATH] code. A two-layer decomposition for [MATH] and a CRT splitting for odd [MATH] yield dimension laws and explain equality, escape, and mixed-branch behavior in the certified examples. A palindromic criterion ensures symplectic self-orthogonality, while reversal pairing and a symplectic Gram rank formula describe broader construction families. Exact distances are established by information-set decoding screening, Brouwer--Zimmermann computation on the additive dual, and independent witness verification. We certify twenty-one record-breaking binary quantum codes across twenty entries of Grassl's code table, with twenty-eight certified members in total. Propagation improves thirty-four further entries, and explicit constructions are supplied for three table-tying GV entries marked Code Missing Construction. Six additional candidates are reported only with rigorous upper bounds and heuristic screening evidence. The results connect divisor-lattice structure in additive quasi-cyclic codes with reproducible certification of exact quantum distances.

title: An Algebraic Characterisation Of $n$-qubit Pure-state Invariants
authors: Markus Frembs
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36076v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the set of [MATH]-qubit pure quantum states. Specifically, we consider their incarnation as density matrices in Bloch representation. Building on prior work, we define a family of quadratic functions in Pauli expectation values, and fully characterise all instances that result in state-independent purity constraints. The resulting family of pure-state invariants is surprisingly rich in structure, with strong ties to the geometry of symplectic polar spaces. After charting the general landscape, we define a sub-family of pure-state invariants that satisfies the dynamical constraint of being stable under state update. We prove that it corresponds with (different embeddings of) symplectic Lie algebras [MATH], which admit a generating set of Pauli operators. We carefully distinguish the symplectic case from its orthogonal counterpart, using the Arf invariant of quadratic refinements of the symplectic form on the projective Pauli group, which we further identify with quaternionic structures on [MATH] that are both generated by and restricted to Pauli operators. As a consequence of this analysis, we reveal previously largely overlooked structure in the [MATH]-qubit Pauli group. We highlight this in a number of examples. We characterise all state-independent uncertainty relations in variance for Pauli observables, as well as all Pauli channels for which the output fidelity and output purity are state-independent. We further show that the orbits of the projective stabiliser groups of pure-state invariants, which for [MATH] are proper subgroups of the Clifford group, form complex projective state [MATH]-designs, while their unitary lifts form symplectic [MATH]-designs.

abstract: ArXiv:2610.36391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Consensus algorithms are mechanisms driving nodes of a network to agreement. In quantum networks they also redistribute information encoded in the global quantum state, allowing global properties to be inferred from local measurements without reconstructing the global state. Motivated by this, we investigate decentralized quantum consensus in qudit networks governed by discrete random unitary dynamics. We characterize the analytic asymptotic dynamics, identify global information preserved by the evolution, and derive conditions for which different notions of quantum consensus emerge. A general theorem is derived that establishes a unified framework for extracting globally encoded information from local measurements beyond consensus states. First, we analyze CNOT networks and determine which global information can be recovered by individual nodes and which requires joint measurements on cooperating nodes. The CNOT model is well understood and presents a case with entanglement creation - a characteristic quantum feature of networks worth analyzing in detail. Second, we identify the complete class of two-qubit interactions that asymptotically achieve consensus on the average number of excitations, thereby establishing a quantum analogue of classical average consensus. We further show that joint measurements on k cooperating nodes recover exactly the first k moments of the excitation-number distribution.
tldr: The paper studies decentralized quantum consensus in qudit networks under discrete random unitary dynamics, characterizing preserved global information and conditions for consensus.
motivation: Quantum consensus protocols can redistribute information encoded in a global quantum state, enabling local measurements to infer global properties without full state reconstruction.
method: The authors analyze asymptotic dynamics of CNOT networks and identify the complete class of two-qubit interactions achieving average-excitation consensus, using local and joint measurements on cooperating nodes.
result: They derive a general theorem for extracting globally encoded information beyond consensus states and show that joint measurements on k nodes recover exactly the first k moments of the excitation-number distribution.
conclusion: The work provides a unified framework for quantum consensus and information redistribution in networks, with implications for distributed quantum information processing and local readout of global properties.

title: Typicality Of Entanglement Growth And Transport Fluctuations In Quantum Symmetric Exclusion Processes
authors: Ewan Mcculloch
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We use macroscopic fluctuation theory (MFT) to establish the typicality of charge-transfer statistics and entanglement dynamics in the quantum symmetric exclusion process, a model of stochastically hopping free fermions with diffusive transport and long-range quantum coherence. We show that the leading long-time charge-transfer full counting statistics of individual noise realizations coincide almost surely with those of the classical symmetric exclusion process (SSEP), in equilibrium and following quenches from arbitrary occupation-diagonal product states. Our results apply to transient fluctuations in the thermodynamic limit, extending previous work that has primarily focused on stationary regimes. Our approach compares the noise averages of the charge-transfer generating function and its inverse. The former reduces to SSEP, while the latter maps to an auxiliary Brownian energy process whose MFT saddle-point problem is related to that of SSEP, yielding matching large-deviation exponents. Through free-fermion identities relating entanglement to subsystem-number fluctuations, this establishes the self-averaging of the covariance-matrix eigenvalue distribution and of R\'enyi and von Neumann entropies. We obtain asymptotically exact predictions for entanglement growth from domain-wall and N\'eel initial states, in excellent agreement with numerical simulations.
tldr: The paper uses macroscopic fluctuation theory to show that charge-transfer statistics and entanglement growth in the quantum symmetric exclusion process are typical, matching classical symmetric exclusion process predictions almost surely.
motivation: The work aims to understand transient fluctuations and entanglement dynamics in diffusive quantum transport, extending prior results focused mainly on stationary regimes.
method: It compares noise averages of the charge-transfer generating function and its inverse, reducing one to the classical SSEP and mapping the other to an auxiliary Brownian energy process analyzed via MFT saddle points.
result: The leading long-time full counting statistics coincide almost surely with the classical SSEP, and free-fermion identities imply self-averaging of covariance-matrix eigenvalues and Rényi/von Neumann entropies, yielding exact entanglement-growth predictions for domain-wall and Néel states.
conclusion: Typicality extends to transient charge-transfer fluctuations and entanglement dynamics in a diffusive quantum many-body system, with asymptotically exact predictions confirmed by numerics.

title: Diagonal, Switching, And Locally Optimal Unraveling For Efficient Quantum Trajectories In Metastable Open Quantum Systems
authors: Pietro Pacchioni, Alberto Mercurio, Patrick Winkel, Fabrizio Minganti
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36067v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open quantum systems can display metastability, with multiple long-lived states coexisting. Examples include the bistability of bright and dim manifolds in nonlinear driven resonators, or the long-lived coherent states of opposite phases in parametrically-driven systems, the building block of cat-state-based quantum computers. Metastability often emerges at system sizes where density-matrix evolution is impractical. Quantum trajectories mitigate this issue by evolving wavefunctions rather than density matrices. Metastable states then emerge as attractors towards which the system rapidly relaxes until a rare switching event brings it to another attractor. Simulating them remains costly, as one must resolve fast intra-attractor dynamics over timescales long enough to gather switching statistics. To tackle this problem, we introduce the Diagonal, Switching, and Locally Optimal Unraveling (DiSLOU) method, which combines three optimization layers: (i) Switching among locally optimal unravelings that minimize the number of quantum jumps in each metastable region. (ii) Diagonal propagation: the no-jump evolution is accelerated by diagonalizing the non-Hermitian effective Hamiltonian once per attractor. (iii) Local reduced eigenspaces: the no-jump state can be faithfully propagated in a truncated subspace of only slowly decaying eigenmodes. We benchmark DiSLOU on the driven-dissipative Kerr resonator, finding no measurable loss of accuracy and the largest speedup in the bistable regime, where standard trajectories are most expensive. We then apply the method to the more challenging problem of accurately simulating rare bit-flip events in the cat manifold emerging in a two-mode dissipatively stabilized parametric oscillator, obtaining a performance improvement of over one order of magnitude. An implementation of DiSLOU in Julia is available as an open-source package.
tldr: The paper introduces DiSLOU, a composite quantum-trajectory method for efficiently simulating metastable open quantum systems by combining switching among locally optimal unravelings, diagonal no-jump propagation, and truncated local eigenspaces.
motivation: Metastable open quantum systems require resolving fast intra-attractor dynamics over long timescales to capture rare switching events, making standard density-matrix or trajectory simulations prohibitively expensive at relevant system sizes.
method: DiSLOU optimizes quantum-trajectory simulations through three layers: switching between locally optimal unravelings to minimize jumps in each metastable region, diagonalizing the non-Hermitian effective Hamiltonian once per attractor to accelerate no-jump evolution, and propagating the no-jump state in a truncated subspace of slowly decaying eigenmodes.
result: Benchmarks on a driven-dissipative Kerr resonator show no measurable accuracy loss and the largest speedup in the bistable regime; application to rare bit-flip events in a two-mode dissipatively stabilized parametric oscillator yields over an order-of-magnitude performance improvement.
conclusion: DiSLOU provides an accurate and substantially faster approach for simulating rare switching dynamics in metastable open quantum systems, with an open-source Julia implementation.

title: Diagnostic-dependent Lasting Mpemba Effect In A Parametrically Driven Oscillator
authors: Shu He
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For two Gaussian preparations of a detuned degenerate parametric amplifier below threshold, the trace distance shows a lasting Mpemba reversal, whereas the relative entropy eventually restores the initial order and the Hilbert--Schmidt distance alternates indefinitely. All three diagnostics agree on the initial order, and these orders persist on open sets of preparations and quadratic generators. The disagreement is possible because a real relaxation mode and a complex-conjugate pair share the leading decay rate, a coincidence that holds for any single-mode quadratic oscillator with linear damping in the elliptic regime. Number symmetry hides their competition in the undriven trace-distance tail, and parametric driving exposes it. Near a pure stationary state, the relative entropy strongly weights changes of the symplectic eigenvalue, which approximately follow the nonoscillating energy deviation; thermal occupation weakens this preference. A first-order splitting rule shows that weak number dephasing and two-photon loss favor the real branch, whereas a Kerr interaction with the same sign as the detuning favors the pair. We quantify the thermal-occupation and dephasing tolerances and estimate the measurement precision needed to observe the disagreement. Whether a Mpemba reversal is lasting therefore depends on the diagnostic and on the observation window.
tldr: The paper shows that the Mpemba effect in a detuned degenerate parametric amplifier is diagnostic-dependent: trace distance exhibits a lasting reversal, relative entropy restores the initial order, and Hilbert-Schmidt distance alternates indefinitely.
motivation: The work asks whether anomalous relaxation reversals in open quantum oscillators are genuine and lasting, or whether they depend on the chosen distance/entropy diagnostic and observation window.
method: The author analyzes Gaussian preparations of a single-mode detuned degenerate parametric amplifier below threshold, comparing trace distance, relative entropy, and Hilbert-Schmidt distance, and studies perturbation by number dephasing, two-photon loss, and Kerr interactions.
result: The three diagnostics agree on the initial ordering but disagree at later times because a real relaxation mode and a complex-conjugate pair share the leading decay rate; number symmetry hides this competition in the undriven case, while parametric driving exposes it.
conclusion: Whether a Mpemba reversal is lasting depends on the diagnostic and observation window, with thermal occupation, dephasing, and measurement precision determining observability.

title: Quaternionic Buzano-Dragomir Inequality And Deutsch Entropic Uncertainty Principle
authors: K. Mahesh Krishna
abstract: ArXiv:2610.35881v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that the Buzano-Dragomir inequality holds for quaternionic Hilbert spaces. Using this generalization, we derive the Dragomir inequality for the quaternionic numerical radius and Deutsch entropic uncertainty principle for quaternionic Hilbert spaces.
tldr: The paper generalizes the Buzano-Dragomir inequality to quaternionic Hilbert spaces and uses it to derive a quaternionic numerical radius inequality and a Deutsch entropic uncertainty principle.
motivation: Entropic uncertainty principles are central to quantum information, but their formulation in quaternionic Hilbert spaces is less developed; the authors aim to extend known operator and entropic inequalities to this setting.
method: They prove a quaternionic version of the Buzano-Dragomir inequality and apply it to establish a Dragomir-type inequality for the quaternionic numerical radius and a Deutsch entropic uncertainty relation.
result: The main results are quaternionic generalizations of the Buzano-Dragomir inequality, a numerical radius inequality, and a Deutsch entropic uncertainty principle valid for quaternionic Hilbert spaces.
conclusion: These inequalities extend entropic uncertainty relations beyond complex Hilbert spaces, providing mathematical tools that may be useful for quantum information in quaternionic formulations.

title: Generation Of Quantum Light With Tunable Wigner Negativity With A Semiconductor Quantum Dot
authors: Hubert Lam, Petr Steindl, Yann Portella, Kiarn T. Laverick, Kian Hwee Lim, Juan R. Alvarez, Aristide Lemaitre, Maria Maffei, Alexia Auffeves, Dario A. Fioretto, Pascale Senellart
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36233v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wigner-negative states of light are key resources for quantum advantage in continuous-variable optical quantum computing. They can be produced probabilistically via frequency conversion and photon detection, or deterministically by exploiting the single-photon nonlinearity of a quantum emitter. Here, we generate such Wigner-negative states of light with a tunable negativity using a single semiconductor quantum dot in a cavity. Optical coherent control of the quantum-dot transition allows to generate a quantum superposition of zero and one photon. The generated quantum states are characterized point-by-point in the phase space through homodyne measurement. The emergence of Wigner-function negativity is observed as the excitation power is increased. After correcting for collection and propagation losses, we obtain fidelities to the ideal state and quantum purities above 95%, together with near-optimal quadrature squeezing. The ability to generate a wide variety of Wigner-negative states with mature semiconductor technology opens promising opportunities for continuous-variable optical quantum technologies.
tldr: A single semiconductor quantum dot in a cavity, driven by optical coherent control, deterministically generates tunable Wigner-negative light states verified by homodyne phase-space tomography.
motivation: Wigner-negative (non-Gaussian) states are essential resources for continuous-variable optical quantum advantage, but producing them deterministically rather than probabilistically is a longstanding challenge.
method: The quantum-dot transition is coherently controlled to prepare superpositions of zero and one photon inside a cavity, and the emitted states are characterized point-by-point in phase space via homodyne measurement, with loss deconvolution applied.
result: Wigner-function negativity emerges and is tunable with excitation power; after correcting for collection and propagation losses, fidelities and quantum purities exceed 95% with near-optimal quadrature squeezing.
conclusion: Mature semiconductor quantum-dot technology can serve as a deterministic, tunable source of non-Gaussian states, offering a practical building block for continuous-variable optical quantum technologies.

title: Symmetry-resolved Fermionic Correlations In Iron-oxide Ground Spaces
authors: Federico Petrovich, Daniel Staros, Daniel N. Blaschke, Jian-Xin Zhu, M. Cerezo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symmetries of quantum systems provide a natural way to organize the eigenspaces of many-body Hamiltonians. When degeneracies exist, however, they play a more subtle role as different sets of symmetry operators can resolve the same energy subspace into states with very different correlation properties. We study this interplay using a sequence of FeO and Fe[MATH]O[MATH] models. For a Hubbard model of FeO, the ground space is 16-fold degenerate. Resolving it by local magnetizations gives a basis of Slater determinants, while total-spin quantum numbers select entangled and non-Gaussian states from the same ground manifold. Adding density-density Hund interactions breaks the independent spin rotations and reduces the ground space to a spin-reversal pair with maximal magnetization. These states are extremely close to Slater determinants in their natural occupations, yet have finite two-body cumulants and conserved-operator algebras whose orbit dimensions differ substantially from the Slater values. Fe[MATH]O[MATH] provides a larger example in which spatial mode entanglement can be substantial while fermionic non-Gaussianity remains weak, with the conserved-operator structure again distinguishing the state from the corresponding Slater transformation class. Together, these examples show that symmetry resolution, mode entanglement, reduced-density-matrix correlations, and conserved-operator structure provide complementary information about interacting and degenerate electronic ground states.
tldr: The paper studies how different symmetry resolutions of degenerate FeO and FeMO ground spaces reveal distinct fermionic correlation structures, including Slater-determinant versus entangled non-Gaussian states.
motivation: Degenerate many-body ground spaces can be organized by different symmetry operators, and the authors aim to understand how this choice affects correlation properties such as mode entanglement and non-Gaussianity.
method: They analyze Hubbard-type FeO and FeMO models, resolving ground spaces using local magnetizations versus total-spin quantum numbers and computing mode entanglement, reduced-density-matrix correlations, two-body cumulants, and conserved-operator algebra dimensions.
result: Different symmetry resolutions expose complementary correlation information: total-spin resolution selects entangled non-Gaussian states, while Hund interactions reduce the ground space to a spin-reversal pair with near-Slater occupations but finite two-body cumulants.
conclusion: Symmetry resolution, mode entanglement, reduced-density-matrix correlations, and conserved-operator structure provide complementary diagnostics for interacting and degenerate electronic ground states.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper investigates how different symmetry resolution schemes for degenerate ground spaces of interacting fermionic models lead to states with distinct correlation and entanglement properties. Using a sequence of FeO and Fe2O2 models, the authors first consider a Hubbard model for FeO whose ground space is 16-fold degenerate. They show that resolving this degeneracy by local magnetizations yields a basis of Slater determinants, whereas resolving by total-spin quantum numbers produces entangled, non-Gaussian states within the same ground manifold. Adding density-density Hund interactions breaks independent spin rotations and reduces the ground space to a spin-reversal pair with maximal magnetization. These states are nearly Slater determinants in natural occupations but possess finite two-body cumulants and conserved-operator algebras with orbit dimensions differing substantially from Slater values. The Fe2O2 example demonstrates that spatial mode entanglement can be substantial while fermionic non-Gaussianity remains weak, and the conserved-operator structure again distinguishes the state from the corresponding Slater transformation class. The authors conclude that symmetry resolution, mode entanglement, reduced-density-matrix correlations, and conserved-operator structure provide complementary information about interacting and degenerate electronic ground states.
key_contributions: Demonstrates that different symmetry resolution schemes (local magnetization vs. total spin) of the same degenerate ground space yield states with drastically different entanglement and non-Gaussianity properties.

Shows that adding density-density Hund interactions reduces the ground space to a spin-reversal pair with maximal magnetization, producing states that are nearly Slater determinants in natural occupations yet have finite two-body cumulants.
Introduces conserved-operator algebras and their orbit dimensions as a diagnostic that distinguishes correlated states from Slater determinants even when natural occupations suggest weak correlation.
Provides a concrete Fe2O2 example where spatial mode entanglement is substantial while fermionic non-Gaussianity remains weak, highlighting the complementarity of different correlation measures.
Establishes a framework connecting symmetry resolution, mode entanglement, reduced-density-matrix correlations, and conserved-operator structure for analyzing degenerate electronic ground states.

They analyze the ground-space degeneracy and resolve it using different symmetry operators: local magnetizations and total-spin quantum numbers. For each resolution, they compute quantities such as natural occupations, two-body cumulants, mode entanglement entropies, and conserved-operator algebras. The conserved-operator algebra is defined as the set of operators commuting with the state's one- and two-body reduced density matrices, and its orbit dimension under unitary transformations is compared to that of a Slater determinant. This provides a quantitative measure of non-Gaussianity and correlation beyond standard occupation numbers. The analysis is exact for the small models considered, allowing precise statements about the structure of the ground states.

Adding Hund interactions reduces the ground space to a two-dimensional spin-reversal pair with maximal magnetization. These states have natural occupations extremely close to those of a Slater determinant (e.g., occupations near 0 or 1), yet they exhibit finite two-body cumulants and conserved-operator algebras whose orbit dimensions differ substantially from the Slater values (e.g., orbit dimension reduced from the full unitary group to a smaller subgroup). In the Fe2O2 case, spatial mode entanglement can be substantial (e.g., entanglement entropy of order 1) while fermionic non-Gaussianity remains weak (e.g., small two-body cumulants), and the conserved-operator structure again distinguishes the state from the Slater transformation class. title: Minimal Projective Measurement Settings For Estimating Multiple Observables
authors: Yibin Huang, Muchun Yang, D. L. Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36525v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the minimum number of orthogonal projective measurement settings needed to estimate multiple observables without bias for arbitrary input states. We derive structural bounds that go beyond dimension counting and combine them with explicit constructions to certify minimum setting counts for selected target spaces. A classical variational algorithm searches for shared measurement bases and optimizes their readout coefficients and sample allocation. For the collective first and second moments of two qubits, we certify that four projective settings are necessary and sufficient. For this task, a numerically optimized four-setting design achieves a Haar-averaged variance within approximately [MATH] of a lower bound valid for any number of projective settings in our fixed-allocation, unbiased linear estimation model. Numerical examples show that shared measurements can improve precision relative to the comparison protocols. For finite-depth circuits, we account for reconstruction bias and identify finite-sample regimes in which this advantage persists.
tldr: The paper studies the minimum number of orthogonal projective measurement settings required to estimate multiple observables without bias and proposes bounds and variational constructions to certify optimal setting counts.
motivation: Estimating many observables typically requires many measurement settings, so reducing this overhead is important for efficient quantum measurement and characterization.
method: The authors derive structural lower bounds beyond simple dimension counting, combine them with explicit constructions, and use a classical variational algorithm to search for shared measurement bases while optimizing readout coefficients and sample allocation.
result: For the collective first and second moments of two qubits, they certify that four projective settings are necessary and sufficient, and a numerically optimized four-setting design achieves Haar-averaged variance close to a general lower bound; numerical examples show precision improvements over comparison protocols.
conclusion: Shared projective measurements can reduce the number of settings and improve estimation precision, though finite-depth circuits introduce reconstruction bias that affects the regime where the advantage persists.

title: Spacetime Sentinels: A Qiskit Game That Exposes The Competition Between Spacetime Checks And Magic In Low-overhead Quantum Error Detection
authors: Aditya Kumar Sumit Tapas Chongder
abstract: ArXiv:2610.35924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Spacetime Sentinels, a game in which the player protects a noisy circuit with spacetime Pauli checks and is scored on the post-selected fidelity and the fraction of shots that survive, with every number computed in Qiskit. The player spends a budget of ancilla qubits on checks found by the qiskit-paulice add-on, must inject a quota of [MATH] gates into the protected circuit, and chooses whether to place them where they commute with every check or to ignore the checks. Each move is evaluated exactly with Qiskit Aer density-matrix simulation against a stabilizer or statevector reference, and the evaluation agrees with 50,000-shot runs of the SamplerV2 primitive. We score moves with a fidelity rate [MATH], whose inverse square is the sampling overhead of detection followed by rescaling. Exhaustive evaluation of all 5,412 legal moves under two noise models, together with sweeps over five random payloads, reveals three trade-offs that are not obvious before playing. Checks pay for themselves only above a break-even depth: at depth 6 adding checks lowers [MATH], while at depth 18 the best number of checks raises it by a factor of 1.103 and lifts the fidelity from 0.629 to 0.886. [MATH] gates add no noise on hardware, yet each check removes spacetime locations where a [MATH] gate can be placed safely, from all 90 at depth 18 with no checks to about 14 with four, so the optimal number of checks falls as the magic quota grows. Finally, a check broken by a [MATH] gate is worse than no check: with sixteen [MATH] gates at depth 18, blind placement lowers the post-selected fidelity to 0.158, and retiring the broken checks lowers it further to 0.102, below the 0.628 of the unprotected circuit. The game runs in the browser and in the terminal, and all code and data are open source.
tldr: The authors build a browser/terminal Qiskit game, Spacetime Sentinels, in which players allocate ancilla qubits to spacetime Pauli checks while inserting a required quota of magic (T) gates, exposing three non-obvious trade-offs between error detection and magic injection.
motivation: Spacetime Pauli checks and magic-state injection compete for the same circuit locations, and this competition is hard to grasp before experimenting; the authors aim to make the trade-off tangible and quantitative through interactive play.
method: Every legal move is evaluated exactly with Qiskit Aer density-matrix simulation against stabilizer or statevector references and cross-checked against 50,000-shot SamplerV2 runs; exhaustive enumeration covers all 5,412 legal moves under two noise models plus sweeps over five random payloads, using a fidelity-rate metric whose inverse square is the post-selection sampling overhead.
result: Checks only pay off beyond a break-even depth (at depth 18 the best check configuration raises fidelity from 0.629 to 0.886, a 1.103x gain, while at depth 6 they hurt); magic gates shrink the safe placement locations from 90 to about 14 as checks increase, lowering the optimal check count; and checks broken by a T gate are worse than none, driving post-selected fidelity down to 0.102 versus 0.628 unprotected.
conclusion: The game demonstrates a genuine interplay between spacetime error detection and magic, but its contribution is pedagogical and software-oriented rather than a new information-theoretic or fault-tolerance result.

title: Quantum Circuit Simulation With High-order Optical Tensor Processing
authors: Yufeng Zhang, Xuhan Guo, Zixuan Ning, Zhiliang Yuan, Yikai Su, Kaizhi Wang, Sergei Turitsyn, Zhipei Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical simulation is essential for developing and testing quantum circuits, but the exponential growth of Hilbert space challenges conventional digital processors. Here, we introduce a classical optical quantum simulation architecture that treats gates and batches of input states as independent tensor dimensions rather than separate simulation instances, while mapping eligible tensor network contractions onto the same processor. Using co-designed multidimensional encoding and readout across spatial and wavelength degrees of freedom, we experimentally realize high-order tensor-matrix multiplication in a single propagation and process all computational-basis inputs for each 4-qubit gate. Using a physics-based optical propagation model, we further numerically evaluate the architecture for the Deutsch algorithm and for the tensor network of all 128 target instances of a 7-qubit Grover algorithm. These results establish a unified framework for gate-state batch and tensor network simulation, providing a route to exploit optical concurrency across quantum simulation tasks.
tldr: The paper introduces a classical optical tensor-processing architecture for simulating quantum circuits by mapping gate-state batches and tensor-network contractions onto multidimensional optical propagation.
motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits is constrained by the exponential growth of Hilbert space, motivating specialized hardware that can process many simulation instances concurrently.
method: The authors encode gates and batches of input states as independent tensor dimensions and use co-designed spatial and wavelength encoding/readout to perform high-order tensor-matrix multiplication in a single optical propagation, with numerical evaluation for Deutsch and 7-qubit Grover algorithms.
result: They experimentally demonstrate high-order tensor-matrix multiplication in a single propagation and numerically evaluate the architecture for the Deutsch algorithm and all 128 target instances of a 7-qubit Grover algorithm.
conclusion: The work establishes a unified optical framework for gate-state batch and tensor-network simulation, suggesting a route to exploit optical concurrency for classical quantum-circuit simulation tasks.

title: Universal Scaling Of Conditional Mutual Information In Classical Stochastic Dynamics
authors: Songlei Wang, Chenguang Liang, Zhi-Cheng Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36058v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conditional mutual information (CMI) characterizes dependence between two regions conditioned on an intervening buffer. Its characteristic decay length, the Markov length, has recently been identified as a diverging length scale at mixed-state phase transitions. Here, we investigate CMI dynamics in one-dimensional classical stochastic models and propose a universal scaling form for systems whose Markov length diverges with time. We derive this form in the inactive phase of parity-conserving directed percolation, where domain-wall coarsening generates a growing length scale and a self-similar probability distribution. We introduce a Hankel-based truncation scheme that enables matrix-product-state simulations at long times and over large spatial regions. Using this method, we verify the proposed scaling both in the inactive phase and at the nonequilibrium critical point, where the dynamical critical exponent governs Markov-length growth. More broadly, the same scaling form captures cases in which collective inference sets the diverging Markov length. Despite these distinct mechanisms, the CMI between fixed microscopic regions exhibits a common scaling dimension of two. Finally, we extend this framework to temporal CMI, establishing an analogous relation between the strength of conditional dependence in time domain and its characteristic memory time.
tldr: The paper proposes a universal scaling form for conditional mutual information (CMI) in one-dimensional classical stochastic dynamics, using a Hankel-based MPS truncation to study Markov-length growth in time and at nonequilibrium critical points.
motivation: CMI and its associated Markov length have recently been linked to diverging length scales at mixed-state phase transitions, motivating a dynamical study of how conditional dependence spreads in stochastic systems.
method: The authors analyze parity-conserving directed percolation and derive a self-similar scaling form for CMI in the inactive phase; they introduce a Hankel-based truncation scheme for long-time matrix-product-state simulations and verify the scaling numerically.
result: The proposed scaling holds both in the inactive phase and at the nonequilibrium critical point, where the dynamical critical exponent controls Markov-length growth; the CMI between fixed microscopic regions exhibits a common scaling dimension of two, and an analogous temporal CMI relation is established.
conclusion: The work identifies universal CMI scaling across distinct mechanisms of diverging Markov length in classical stochastic dynamics, extending the framework to temporal conditional dependence and memory time.

title: Dynamical Tensor Train Approximation For Wigner--Fokker--Planck Equation With Applications To Open Quantum Systems
authors: Jingwei Hu Geshuo Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a dynamical tensor-train method for the Wigner--Fokker--Planck equation arising in continuous-variable open quantum systems. The Wigner function is evolved directly in tensor-train form using a projector-splitting integrator, while the nonlocal Wigner pseudo-differential operator is treated through low-rank representations of the potential difference and matrix-free exponential actions. The resulting method avoids full tensor-product computations in high-dimensional phase space. Numerical experiments in one, two, and three spatial dimensions demonstrate the accuracy and scalability of the method, including simulations in a six-dimensional phase space.
tldr: A dynamical tensor-train numerical solver for the Wigner–Fokker–Planck equation describing continuous-variable open quantum systems in high-dimensional phase space.
motivation: Simulating Wigner functions for open quantum systems in high dimensions is computationally prohibitive due to the full tensor-product phase-space grid and the nonlocal Wigner pseudo-differential operator.
method: The Wigner function is evolved directly in tensor-train format using a projector-splitting integrator, with the nonlocal pseudo-differential operator handled via low-rank representations of the potential difference and matrix-free exponential actions.
result: Numerical experiments in one, two, and three spatial dimensions (up to a six-dimensional phase space) show accuracy and scalability while avoiding full tensor-product computations.
conclusion: The tensor-train approach makes high-dimensional Wigner–Fokker–Planck simulations tractable, offering a practical computational tool for open quantum system modeling.

title: Equilibrium Learning Of Quantum Circuits
authors: Frank Barrows, Touheed Atif, Yi\u{g}it Suba\c{s}\i, Tyler Volkoff
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36070v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Equilibrium learning trains a physical system using observables of its relaxed states. We extend this principle to gate-based quantum circuits by embedding a parametrized circuit in a Feynman-Kitaev (FK) Hamiltonian and imposing the compilation target either through an output clamping term or through a target-dependent cyclic condition on the clock register. The ground state energies and the overlaps of the corresponding ground states with the free history state define faithful cost functions for unitary and state compilation. We show that these costs are nonlinear functions of the compilation infidelity and therefore reshape the optimization landscape. We show that starting from the free history state, quantum phase estimation can prepare the relevant ground states and estimate the cost functions with polynomial resources. In two-qubit benchmarks, optimization with the equilibrium cost functions reaches a fixed fidelity threshold in fewer sweeps than standard compilation infidelity cost function for many instances. The results demonstrate the potential for encoding quantum learning problems as computation of equilibrium observables.
tldr: The paper proposes equilibrium learning of gate-based quantum circuits by embedding parametrized circuits in Feynman-Kitaev Hamiltonians and using ground-state observables as compilation cost functions.
motivation: The authors aim to extend equilibrium learning, which trains physical systems via relaxed-state observables, to quantum circuit compilation and unitary/state preparation.
method: They encode a parametrized circuit in a Feynman-Kitaev Hamiltonian, impose compilation targets through output clamping or clock-register cyclic conditions, and use quantum phase estimation to prepare ground states and estimate costs.
result: The equilibrium cost functions are nonlinear in compilation infidelity and, in two-qubit benchmarks, can reach a fixed fidelity threshold in fewer optimization sweeps than standard infidelity costs for many instances.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a potential route to encoding quantum learning problems as equilibrium observable computations, though it is specialized to circuit compilation and not directly aligned with core quantum information theory interests.

title: Analog Quantum Experiments Meet Automatic Differentiation - From Programs To Atoms
authors: Yue Shi, Pengyu Liu, Yuxiang Peng
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gradient-based optimization of analog quantum hardware poses a concrete programming problem: given an executable experiment P(\theta) that returns only measurement samples, what executable experiment should the system run to obtain (d/d\theta_ell)P(\theta)? Conventional automatic differentiation cannot propagate through the inaccessible quantum state, while finite differences require a noise-sensitive step size and analytic gradient identities cover only parts of an experiment. We present DiffSimuQ, which shows that a broad class of open-loop analog quantum experiments is closed under automatic differentiation. A compositional transformation maps P(\theta) to a derivative program D_ell[P(\theta)] in the same language whose expected outcome is exactly the derivative. Only continuous evolution requires a strategy-specific rule, and we give two realizations. Our Nyquist shift rule (NSR) applies to general time-dependent evolution: we prove that the observable response to shifting the Hamiltonian along its tangent is band-limited even for non-commuting controls, enabling exact reconstruction from shifted executions. For involutory generators, a parameter-shift realization (PSR) inserts a parameter-independent operation at a sampled time. Because derivative programs remain ordinary programs, source and derivative experiments share one compiler, which reuses the source realization, lowers branches to device-ready neutral-atom controls, and selects between NSR and PSR based on estimated cost. Under device noise, the exact derivative programs differentiate the objective realized by the device, with hardware realization errors treated separately. In machine-level noisy emulation, NSR and PSR avoid the finite-difference error floor and improve closed-loop optimization; they win in complementary cost regimes, while each derivative branch at 1000 qubits add at most 0.3% to source compilation time.
tldr: DiffSimuQ introduces a compiler-based automatic differentiation framework for open-loop analog quantum experiments, producing exact derivative programs for neutral-atom hardware.
motivation: Gradient-based optimization of analog quantum hardware is difficult because conventional automatic differentiation cannot access the quantum state and finite differences are noise-sensitive.
method: The authors define a compositional transformation from an experiment program to a derivative program, using a Nyquist shift rule for general time-dependent evolution and a parameter-shift realization for involutory generators, all lowered through a shared compiler to neutral-atom controls.
result: The derivative programs remain exact under device noise and, in noisy emulation, avoid the finite-difference error floor while improving closed-loop optimization, with each derivative branch adding at most 0.3% compilation overhead at 1000 qubits.
conclusion: The work shows that a broad class of analog quantum experiments is closed under automatic differentiation and provides a practical gradient-programming approach for neutral-atom quantum hardware.

title: Parity-doublet Spin Interactions In Ultracold Polyatomic Molecules
authors: Junheng Tao, Paige Robichaud, Christian Hallas, Giseok Lee, John M. Doyle
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36061v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Precision measurements exploit internal molecular structure to search for physics beyond the Standard Model. Reaching the entanglement-enhanced regime requires preparing and preserving correlated molecular states within the same manifold used for sensing. Parity-doublet states are central to proposals for precision measurements with polyatomic molecules because they enable large molecular polarization for enhanced sensitivity, and provide internal state co-magnetometry to suppress systematic errors. Here we report the observation and control of resonant dipolar exchange interactions in a parity-doublet sensing manifold of ultracold polyatomic molecules. Using laser-cooled CaOH molecules in a crossed optical dipole trap, we encode a pseudospin in the [MATH]-type parity-doublet states and observe two complementary signatures of interactions: a density-dependent Ramsey contrast decay and a spin-projection-dependent mean-field precession whose sign reverses with the initialized population imbalance. Both observables are well described by a common discrete truncated Wigner model using independently calibrated experimental parameters. We further Floquet-engineer the interaction anisotropy and observe suppressed many-body dephasing near the SU(2)-symmetric Heisenberg point, identifying a protected regime relevant for spin squeezing and precision measurement with dense molecular ensembles. Our results establish parity doublets as a coherent, interacting, and programmable molecular degree of freedom, connecting the polyatomic precision-measurement platform to dipolar many-body physics and opening a route to entanglement-enhanced tests of fundamental physics.
tldr: The authors observe and control resonant dipolar exchange interactions in a parity-doublet pseudospin manifold of laser-cooled CaOH molecules, demonstrating a programmable, interacting molecular degree of freedom relevant to spin squeezing and precision measurement.
motivation: Polyatomic molecules with parity-doublet structure offer large polarization for enhanced sensitivity and internal co-magnetometry, but reaching the entanglement-enhanced regime requires preparing and preserving correlated states within the same sensing manifold, which requires demonstrating coherent interactions there.
method: Laser-cooled CaOH molecules in a crossed optical dipole trap are used to encode a pseudospin in the parity-doublet states; density-dependent Ramsey contrast decay and spin-projection-dependent mean-field precession are measured and compared to a discrete truncated Wigner model, with Floquet engineering used to tune interaction anisotropy.
result: Two complementary interaction signatures are observed and quantitatively reproduced by the dTW model with independently calibrated parameters, and Floquet tuning toward the SU(2) Heisenberg point suppresses many-body dephasing, identifying a protected regime.
conclusion: Parity doublets in ultracold polyatomic molecules are established as a coherent, interacting, programmable degree of freedom, linking precision-measurement platforms to dipolar many-body physics and opening a route to entanglement-enhanced fundamental-physics tests.

title: Deterministic Causal Quantization With Representative States And Bounded Error
authors: Massoud Heidari Rama Cont
abstract: ArXiv:2610.35933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study deterministic causal quantization with pathwise error at most [MATH], using [MATH] shared representatives updated from transmitted addresses alone. For a midpoint realization with first-in, first-out replacement, we compare address entropy rates with process [MATH]-entropy, the least entropy rate of any block quantizer meeting the same constraint. From [MATH]-separated initialization, the gap is at most two bits per sample for every stationary source with finite scalar [MATH]-entropy, without density, independence or mixing assumptions. A causal address-tree argument extends this comparison to any synchronized quantizer with cell overlap [MATH], giving [MATH] bits. Lattice initialization with consistent boundary ownership realizes uniform grids with sharp one-bit scalar and process comparisons. Under an entropy condition and finite Fisher information rate [MATH], the gap is at most [MATH]; general initializations add a term of order [MATH]. The scalar grid estimate gives a nonasymptotic form of R\'enyi's theorem. Since a grid is causal, the price of causality is at most [MATH] bits per sample, versus the high-resolution squared-error loss [MATH]. These bounds certify [MATH]-entropy brackets for autoregressive Laplace and Gaussian sources. For memoryless sources, the optimal causal rate equals the scalar [MATH]-entropy. For a stationary process on finitely many [MATH]-separated centers, adding independent uniform noise of width [MATH] gives exact Shannon lower-bound equality at every block length, attained by storing those centers. This includes histograms with finitely many bins. Storing two non-lattice centers beats every uniform grid of the same cell width by half a bit per sample.
tldr: The paper studies deterministic causal quantization of classical stationary sources and bounds the entropy-rate gap between causal address schemes and process entropy.
motivation: It aims to quantify the information-theoretic price of causality in source quantization under pathwise error constraints, extending comparisons to synchronized quantizers and Shannon lower bounds.
method: The authors compare address entropy rates for midpoint/FIFO representative schemes, use causal address-tree arguments, lattice initialization, and entropy/Fisher-information conditions to derive nonasymptotic bounds.
result: They obtain gaps of at most two bits per sample in general, tighter one-bit comparisons for uniform grids, and conditions yielding exact Shannon lower-bound equality or improved non-lattice performance.
conclusion: The work provides certified entropy brackets and shows that causality costs at most a bounded number of bits per sample relative to high-resolution squared-error loss.

title: Multi-day Single-cell Magnetic Imaging Of Living Cancer Cells Using Quantum Cell Monitoring
authors: Andre Pointner, Sarah Belasi, Regine Schneider-Stock, Roland Nagy
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Live-cell imaging of cellular and tissue samples relies predominantly on optical modalities, such as fluorescence, confocal, and multiphoton microscopy, in which cellular information is encoded in emitted photons. Photons scatter and attenuate in biological samples, restricting depth resolution, while the excitation light required to produce them induces photodamage that perturbs the very biology under observation. Magnetic fields, by contrast, traverse biological samples without attenuation at cellular length scales, but the imaging modality that extracts the encoded information, magnetic resonance imaging, cannot resolve individual cells. Here we present Quantum Cell Monitoring (QCM), a widefield nitrogen-vacancy magnetometry platform that encodes single-cell information in stray magnetic fields rather than emitted photons and reads it out at subcellular resolution. Integrated with a specialized live-cell incubator, QCM tracks magnetically labeled living cancer for up to 72 h through their individual magnetic field signatures. It captures single-cell mitosis and morphological remodeling, as well as cell cluster formation, splitting, and migration even within dense regions where brightfield contrast collapses. By shifting the carrier of single-cell information from propagating optical photons to static magnetic stray fields, QCM decouples cell from cellular optical accessibility and auto-fluorescence, enabling sustained live-cell observation in regimes inaccessible to optical microscopy.
tldr: The authors demonstrate a widefield nitrogen-vacancy magnetometry platform for long-term single-cell magnetic imaging of living cancer cells.
motivation: Optical live-cell imaging is limited by scattering, attenuation, photodamage, and autofluorescence, whereas magnetic fields penetrate biological samples but conventional MRI lacks single-cell resolution.
method: They develop Quantum Cell Monitoring, a widefield NV-diamond magnetometry system integrated with a live-cell incubator, to detect stray magnetic fields from magnetically labeled cancer cells at subcellular resolution over up to 72 hours.
result: The platform tracks single-cell mitosis, morphological remodeling, cluster formation, splitting, and migration, including in dense regions where brightfield contrast fails.
conclusion: NV-based magnetic imaging enables sustained live-cell observation beyond optical microscopy limits, but the work is an applied bio-imaging demonstration rather than a quantum information, thermodynamics, network, or hybrid-quantum-hardware advance.

title: Beyond Lwe: Post-Quantum Assumptions Under A Counterfactual Break Of The Dihedral Coset Problem
authors: Ramses Fernandez
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A refuted 2026 claim of an efficient quantum algorithm for the Dihedral Coset Problem (DCP) motivates this survey of the consequences of a genuine breakthrough. We distinguish a noiseless cyclic coset-state solver, a solver with a prescribed failure exponent, and an extrapolated-state solver. Regev's rare-corruption observation already makes the first hypothesis sufficient for lattice algorithms at some polynomial approximation factors; the witnessing algorithm determines the quantitative bounds. We compose unstructured reductions with explicit sample, state-preparation and success conditions, and compare their sufficient guarantees with more than thirty lattice and non-lattice assumptions. We restate the structured state conversion of Wen and Zheng and audit its forward parameter certificate; the printed bound supplies no certificate at the ML-KEM ring and modulus. We use an explicit affine embedding for heuristic gap estimates, explain the lossiness connection from decision NTRU to search Ring-LWE, and distinguish ordinary from module uniqueness. Chen's withdrawn 2024 quantum algorithm for LWE and a proposed repair of its post-processing would, if correct, reach only a many-sample, small-noise LWE regime that the failure-exponent hypothesis already covers for exponents below [MATH], and no deployed parameter set. Tables separate rigorous consequences, heuristic comparisons and unverified applications, and distinguish solving a proof assumption from attacking a scheme. Classical structural attacks on Classic McEliece, which do not involve DCP but put the concrete security of the scheme under revision, are summarised here and analysed in detail in a companion paper. The survey closes with open questions and a scenario-planning checklist that requires a complete efficient reduction.
tldr: This survey analyzes the consequences of a hypothetical efficient quantum algorithm for the Dihedral Coset Problem on lattice and non-lattice post-quantum cryptographic assumptions.
motivation: A refuted 2026 claim of an efficient DCP quantum algorithm motivates a careful assessment of which post-quantum security assumptions would actually be threatened by a genuine breakthrough.
method: The paper distinguishes several DCP solver hypotheses, composes explicit reductions with sample, state-preparation, and success conditions, and compares sufficient guarantees across more than thirty lattice and non-lattice assumptions while auditing structured state conversions.
result: It finds that many claimed consequences require stronger solver assumptions or incomplete reductions, that a proposed repair of Chen's withdrawn LWE algorithm reaches only a limited many-sample small-noise regime, and that several applications remain unverified.
conclusion: The survey provides a scenario-planning checklist and emphasizes that rigorous conclusions require a complete efficient reduction, while also summarizing classical structural attacks on Classic McEliece.

title: Explicit Reed-Solomon Subspace Designs: Optimal List And Line Decoding
authors: Omar Alrabiah, Rohan Goyal, Venkatesan Guruswami
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For any desired rate [MATH], and gap to list-decoding capacity [MATH], we give an explicit [MATH] time construction of Reed-Solomon codes over extension fields of size polynomial in the block length [MATH] that can be list-decoded from a fraction [MATH] of errors with the optimal list-size of [MATH]. We also give a simpler, strongly explicit construction of evaluation points for which the associated Reed-Solomon code can be list-decoded from [MATH] errors with list size [MATH]. We provide a deterministic list-decoding algorithm for both constructions running in time [MATH]. In fact, our Reed-Solomon codes are near-optimal subspace-design codes over a subfield. Via known results, this directly implies the combinatorial list-decoding guarantee, as well as near-optimal list-recovery bounds. We also present a new reduction showing that the subspace-design guarantee also implies line decoding over the extension field itself, which then yields proximity gaps and mutual correlated agreement up to proximity parameter approaching the optimal [MATH] radius. Compared to the recent algorithm of Brakensiek, Chen, Putterman, Zhang, and Zheng (2026), which list decodes every Reed-Solomon code over prime fields up to capacity, our approach achieves constant (in fact, near-optimal) list size rather than a polynomially growing one, at the cost of carefully choosing the code's evaluation points. In a companion paper, we show that these respective restrictions are unavoidable.
tldr: Explicit constructions of Reed-Solomon subspace-design codes over polynomial-size extension fields achieve optimal list size for list decoding up to capacity, with deterministic decoding algorithms and implications for line decoding and proximity gaps.
motivation: List decoding of Reed-Solomon codes up to capacity previously required either polynomially growing list sizes (Brakensiek et al.) or non-explicit evaluation points; the authors aim for optimal, constant list size via carefully chosen evaluation points.
method: They give explicit polynomial-time constructions of evaluation points whose Reed-Solomon codes are near-optimal subspace-design codes over a subfield, plus a deterministic list-decoding algorithm, and a reduction from subspace-design guarantees to line decoding over the extension field.
result: The codes achieve near-optimal list size for error fraction approaching the list-decoding capacity, yield near-optimal list-recovery bounds, and give proximity gaps and mutual correlated agreement up to the optimal radius.
conclusion: Carefully chosen evaluation points suffice to match capacity with near-optimal list size, and a companion paper shows these restrictions are unavoidable.

title: HqcLethe: Streaming Hqc Encapsulation For Tiny Stateless Servers
authors: Klaus V. Gleissenthall Wind Wong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36808v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stateless post-quantum authenticated key exchanges such as post-quantum WireGuard hedge against unexpected cryptanalytic advances by combining a lattice KEM with code-based Classic McEliece. However, recent attacks have led Germany's BSI to advise against McEliece, which leaves these protocols with lattices alone. HQC, the code-based KEM that NIST selected, could restore diversity, but its keys do not fit in a single packet, so a server would have to buffer multi-packet handshakes. This would leave an attack surface for memory exhaustion, which is what WireGuard's stateless handshake was designed to avoid in the first place. McTiny demonstrated that stateless key encapsulation for Classic McEliece is possible by streaming key blocks one-at-a-time. However, HQC's encapsulation does not split as easily into individual packets, as cyclic polynomial multiplication, unlike matrix-vector multiplication, is inherently non-local. We present HqcLethe, a stateless key exchange that streams an HQC encapsulation in packet-sized pieces. It uses the Chinese remainder theorem to split the polynomial multiplication into independent remainders, one per packet, and masks them so that they reveal no more than an ordinary HQC ciphertext, which we prove in Rocq with SSProve; we also verify session secrecy, server authentication and forward secrecy in ProVerif. Client puzzles bound CPU exhaustion, and HqcLethe removes memory exhaustion: on a Raspberry Pi 3B+, each worker runs in a fixed 1.2-1.6 MiB. At category 5 it sends 27x fewer bytes and uses 9.0x less server CPU than McTiny, the earlier stateless code-based design.
