method: The authors analyze the Gaussian location model with star-shaped constraints and adversarial contamination, using local entropy and information-theoretic complexity measures to derive minimax lower and upper bounds.
result: They characterize the minimax squared risk as a tradeoff between contamination error and local entropy, showing how these interact as the contamination fraction approaches the breakdown point.
conclusion: The work clarifies the information-theoretic limits of robust constrained mean estimation and provides matching rates across the full contamination regime.

title: Walk On Multiscale Media: Compiling Editable And Composable Transport Medium Prefabs For Monte Carlo Pde Solvers
authors: Xiucheng Li Yunfeng Liao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.35952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monte Carlo PDE solvers enable mesh-free pointwise queries, but repeatedly traversing heterogeneous media is costly, particularly in scenes with reusable or dynamically changing materials. We introduce Walk on Multiscale Media (WoMM), which compiles fine-scale transport into reusable, editable and composable transport prefabs. A probabilistic interpretation of multiscale finite-element bases and condensed operators yields coarse transitions retaining fine-scale material effects. Each prefab combines port-level operators, entrance-dependent exit distributions, and Poisson-marked trajectory records, enabling incremental updates for overlapping absorption fields, gradient-field steering through path reweighting and transient diffusion. Integrated with conventional Walk-on-Spheres in a hybrid continuous--discrete solver, these prefabs accelerate repeated pointwise PDE queries and support interactive material edits without repeatedly solving the fine-scale problem.
tldr: WoMM compiles fine-scale transport behavior in heterogeneous media into reusable, editable, and composable 'transport prefabs' to accelerate repeated Monte Carlo PDE queries.
motivation: Monte Carlo PDE solvers allow mesh-free pointwise queries, but repeatedly traversing heterogeneous or dynamically changing media is computationally expensive, especially when materials are reused or edited.
method: The authors derive a probabilistic interpretation of multiscale finite-element bases and condensed operators to obtain coarse transitions that retain fine-scale material effects, packaging them into prefabs with port-level operators, entrance-dependent exit distributions, and Poisson-marked trajectory records, then integrate them with Walk-on-Spheres in a hybrid continuous-discrete solver.
result: The resulting prefabs support incremental updates for overlapping absorption fields, gradient-field steering via path reweighting, and transient diffusion, accelerating repeated pointwise PDE queries and enabling interactive material edits.
conclusion: Prefab-based compilation of multiscale transport offers an efficient, editable approach to Monte Carlo PDE solving in scenes with reusable or dynamic materials.

title: A Radon-Nikod\'{y}m Theorem For Fuzzy Number Multimeasures In Locally Convex Spaces
authors: Sokol Kaliaj
abstract: ArXiv:2610.35883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we present a Radon-Nikodym theorem for dominated fuzzy number multimeasures defined on [MATH] and taking values in [MATH], where [MATH] is a complete finite measure space and [MATH] is the family of generalized fuzzy numbers on a Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space [MATH], i.e., a map [MATH] is a member of [MATH], if and only if for each [MATH] the [MATH]-cut [MATH] of [MATH] is a member of the family [MATH] of all nonempty convex and weakly compact subsets of [MATH], ([MATH]).
tldr: The paper proves a Radon-Nikodym theorem for dominated fuzzy-number multimeasures taking values in families of generalized fuzzy numbers over a Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space.
motivation: Radon-Nikodym type differentiation results are classical cornerstones of measure theory, and the authors aim to extend them from scalar/set-valued measures to fuzzy-number-valued multimeasures in locally convex settings.
method: The work is purely mathematical functional analysis: generalized fuzzy numbers are characterized via alpha-cuts being nonempty convex weakly compact subsets, and the proof proceeds through measure-theoretic and topological vector space arguments.
result: A Radon-Nikodym derivative (density) is shown to exist for a fuzzy-number multimeasure that is absolutely continuous with respect to a dominating measure on a complete finite measure space.
conclusion: The theorem broadens the scope of Radon-Nikodym theory to fuzzy multimeasures in locally convex spaces, with potential applications in fuzzy decision theory and set-valued analysis rather than in physics.

title: University Research And Leadership In The Age Of Ai: Mobilizing Intellectual Capacity And Building The Infrastructure For Discovery
authors: Bacim Alali
abstract: ArXiv:2610.35919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) raise the prospect of substantial changes in how research is conducted and who can direct discovery. This perspective argues that universities should prepare for these changes by developing AI as well as using it, rather than relying primarily on capabilities designed elsewhere. The relationship is reciprocal: AI can advance disciplinary research, while scientific questions, experimental evidence, and observed failures can guide AI development. The proposal distinguishes three complementary commitments: shared operation of existing AI models, disciplinary AI development, and foundational AI research. Their resource requirements differ, and no single university needs to reproduce a frontier AI company. Shared computational services should be connected to sustained technical teams, laboratory experimentation, and knowledge records that make findings traceable and reusable. Independent evaluation, alignment research, transparent resource allocation, and inclusive academic governance are integral to this infrastructure. Consortia and national facilities can support capabilities beyond individual campuses while preserving room for investigator-led inquiry. Initial programs in experimental and mathematical research would test scientific value, the effort required to validate results, and improvements to AI before expansion. The argument concerns research rather than educational reform and calls for building institutional capacity before the extent and timing of disruption are settled.
tldr: This perspective argues that universities should build institutional capacity to both use and develop AI for scientific research, rather than relying solely on external AI capabilities.
motivation: Advances in AI may reshape how research is conducted and who directs discovery, creating a need for universities to prepare strategically.
method: The paper proposes a conceptual framework with three commitments: shared operation of existing AI models, disciplinary AI development, and foundational AI research, supported by computational services, technical teams, evaluation, alignment research, and governance.
result: It outlines how consortia and national facilities can support capabilities beyond individual campuses while preserving investigator-led inquiry, with initial programs in experimental and mathematical research.
conclusion: The argument calls for universities to build research infrastructure and governance capacity before the extent and timing of AI-driven disruption are settled.

title: When Polynomial Multiplication Counts Geometry: Schubert Polynomials And Monk's Rule
authors: Ryan Bansal
abstract: ArXiv:2610.35944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a geometric introduction to Schubert polynomial multiplication through point-line flags in the complex projective plane. Moving a prescribed point onto a prescribed line gives a family with local equation [MATH], whose limiting curve has two components. The incidence equations and their local multiplicities give a two-term divisor product, using the standard intersection product on classes of algebraic cycles. Permutation labels and Schubert polynomials express the same decomposition as an instance of Monk's rule. For three incidence conditions, each allowing either a point on a prescribed line or a line through a prescribed point, the product has degree six. Under explicit general-position assumptions, direct construction and local equations give six distinct solutions of multiplicity one.
tldr: A geometric exposition of Schubert polynomial multiplication via point-line incidence conditions in the complex projective plane, recovering Monk's rule.
motivation: The author aims to give an intuitive, geometry-first introduction to Schubert polynomial multiplication using concrete enumerative problems of points and lines in CP^2.
method: Moving a prescribed point onto a prescribed line builds a family whose local equation degenerates into a two-component limiting curve; intersection products of incidence cycles and permutation labels yield the Schubert/Monk decomposition, with three incidence conditions producing degree-six enumerative solutions.
result: The two-term divisor product is shown to coincide exactly with Monk's rule on Schubert polynomials, and under explicit general-position assumptions six distinct multiplicity-one solutions are constructed directly.
conclusion: Schubert polynomial structure is exhibited as a transparent geometric counting statement, offering an accessible pedagogical bridge between enumerative geometry and symmetric-function combinatorics.

title: Structured Time-Frequency Representation For Channel Prediction
authors: Ning Yang, Yuming Xian, Tong Li, Ning Gao, Haijun Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.35956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate CSI forecasting is essential for mitigating channel aging and supporting reliable downlink transmission in high-mobility wireless systems. In FDD systems, forecasting future DL CSI from historical UL observations requires joint temporal extrapolation and cross-band inference. However, defining historical UL as the input and future DL as the target does not specify how elapsed time and UL-to-DL band separation should be represented in a pretrained predictor's positional space. FAR-CSI establishes an FDD-aware representation of channel forecasting within a joint temporal and operating-band positional field. Within this field, historical UL observations and future DL targets occupy segregated regions according to their temporal and operating-band roles, preserving the distinction between observed UL context and unobserved DL prediction targets. This representation is instantiated through a unified structured routing rule that governs encoder positional assignment, decoder-field reconstruction, and future-DL target selection, ensuring the same FDD geometry is preserved from contextual encoding to prediction readout. Under matched backbone, initialization, and training conditions, FDD-aware routing reduces NMSE by 21.44\% relative to generic routing. Across the evaluated FDD baselines, FAR-CSI achieves higher CSI prediction accuracy and MRT-based spectral efficiency, while retaining its predictive advantage across mobility conditions, prediction horizons, reduced training-data regimes, and noisy historical observations.
tldr: The paper proposes FAR-CSI, a structured time-frequency positional representation that lets a pretrained predictor distinguish historical uplink observations from future downlink targets for FDD channel-state-information forecasting.
motivation: In FDD high-mobility systems, accurate downlink CSI prediction is needed to combat channel aging, but standard input/target framing does not specify how elapsed time and uplink-downlink band separation should be encoded in a pretrained model's positional space.
method: The authors define a joint temporal and operating-band positional field in which historical UL and future DL occupy segregated regions, and instantiate it through a unified structured routing rule governing encoder positional assignment, decoder-field reconstruction, and future-DL target selection.
result: Under matched backbone, initialization, and training, FDD-aware routing reduces NMSE by 21.44% versus generic routing, and FAR-CSI improves CSI prediction accuracy and MRT-based spectral efficiency across mobility conditions, prediction horizons, data-limited regimes, and noisy observations.
conclusion: Encoding FDD geometry explicitly in the positional representation yields consistent channel-prediction gains, making FAR-CSI a practical approach for reliable downlink transmission in high-mobility FDD systems.

title: Quadratic Reciprocity Via Vandermonde Matrix
authors: Hongshen Chua
abstract: ArXiv:2610.35990v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a proof of the law of quadratic reciprocity using the Vandermonde matrix and Zolotarev's lemma.
tldr: The paper gives a new proof of the law of quadratic reciprocity based on Vandermonde matrices and Zolotarev's lemma.
motivation: Quadratic reciprocity is a central theorem in number theory, and the authors aim to provide an alternative, possibly more elegant, proof using linear-algebraic and permutation-parity tools.
method: The proof combines properties of Vandermonde matrices with Zolotarev's lemma, which relates Legendre symbols to the parity of permutations.
result: A self-contained derivation of the quadratic reciprocity law follows from the Vandermonde/Zolotarev approach.
conclusion: The work is a pure mathematics contribution to number theory with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Finite-Branch Multipliers On A H\"older Algebra: Commutants, Norm Closures, And Essential Spectra
authors: H\"ulya Duru, Serkan \.{i}lter, Arkady Kitover
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36217v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Noninjective multiplication symbols allow commuting operators to mix function values along their fibers, while H\"older regularity constrains this mixing at branch points. We study these operators on the Banach algebra [MATH], [MATH], defined by a restricted interval-variation condition. For [MATH], we determine the full commutant [MATH], including operators whose reflection coefficients need not belong to [MATH]. Separately, we characterize the operator-norm closure [MATH] of the regular multiplication--reflection subalgebra of [MATH], obtain two-sided norm-distance estimates, and find a complemented copy of [MATH] in the Banach-space quotient [MATH]. Every [MATH] satisfies [MATH], and Fredholmness is equivalent to invertibility. For multipliers with finitely many full bi-Lipschitz branches, we also characterize their full commutants and establish the same spectral equalities for every commuting operator. For the regular finite-branch algebra, we establish an exact norm-closure criterion using weighted local H\"older defects and separate row-difference conditions, even when several folds share a level.
tldr: This is a pure functional analysis paper on commutants, norm closures, and Fredholm/spectral properties of finite-branch multiplication-reflection operators on a Hölder algebra.
motivation: The authors study noninjective multiplication symbols that allow commuting operators to mix function values along fibers, with Hölder regularity constraining the mixing at branch points.
method: They work on a Banach algebra defined by a restricted interval-variation condition and characterize commutants, operator-norm closures, quotient structure, and spectral properties for regular finite-branch multipliers.
result: They determine full commutants, obtain norm-distance estimates, find a complemented copy in a Banach-space quotient, prove Fredholmness equals invertibility, and establish exact norm-closure criteria via weighted local Hölder defects.
conclusion: The paper provides a detailed operator-theoretic analysis of multiplication-reflection algebras, but it has no apparent connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Integer Points For Iterated Weierstrass Elliptic Functions
authors: Jane Hawkins
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36323v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Iterated Weierstrass P functions exhibit relationships between period lattices and the dynamics. We connect the dynamical properties to the occurrence of integer and rational points on associated real elliptic curves. Defining a complex number z to be an integer point if both P(z) and P'(z) are integers, we restrict to P when the lattice is real and its invariants g2 and g3 are integers. We study when an integer point lies in the Fatou set of P and when it lies in the Julia set, and if there is any dynamical significance to this. Applying established results on integer solutions to cubic Diophantine equations to the dynamical properties of iterated elliptic P functions, we show integer points at poles of P lie in the Julia set. Integer points can also occur in the Fatou set of P.
tldr: The paper relates integer and rational points on real elliptic curves defined by iterated Weierstrass P functions to their placement in the Fatou or Julia sets of the dynamics.
motivation: Iterated Weierstrass P functions tie period lattices to dynamics, and the authors aim to connect these dynamical properties with arithmetic properties such as integer/rational points on the associated elliptic curves.
method: Defining integer points as those z where both P(z) and P'(z) are integers, the authors restrict to real lattices with integer invariants g2 and g3 and apply established results on integer solutions to cubic Diophantine equations to the dynamics of iterated P.
result: It is shown that integer points located at poles of P lie in the Julia set, while integer points can also occur in the Fatou set.
conclusion: Arithmetic properties of integer points on these elliptic curves have meaningful connections to the dynamical decomposition into Fatou and Julia sets.

title: Pricing Cross-Bank Context In Federated Anti-Money Laundering
authors: Lidia Losavio, Dario Fenoglio, Martin Gjoreski, Marc Langheinrich
abstract: ArXiv:2610.35996v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most graph-based Anti-Money Laundering (AML) methods assume access to a pooled transaction graph containing all accounts and payments, which in reality does not exist. Federated learning offers the necessary privacy guarantees but it remains unclear how money laundering patterns spanning separate graphs can effectively be detected. We exploit transactions already recorded by both endpoint banks to approximate remote account states locally, enabling multi-layer Graph Neural Network (GNN) computation without additional account-specific exchange. Starting from this baseline, we test whether the remaining context is worth sharing, using a disclosure ladder that adds two transaction counts per remote account or the counterparty's own GNN states. On AMLworld HI-Small, across six GNN backbones and up to 32 silos, the observable baseline yields the largest gain and keeps it as fragmentation shrinks the visible slice; counts add a robust correction, while exact remote states help only in specific regimes. In controlled privacy--utility studies, the noise needed to protect shared states erases their detection value before it buys meaningful privacy, whereas counts stay useful even under strong privacy protection. These findings support a practical rule for banks: use what they already record, and formally protect the little that must move.
tldr: This paper studies how cross-bank context can improve federated graph-based anti-money laundering under privacy constraints.
motivation: Most graph-based AML methods assume a pooled transaction graph that does not exist in practice, and it is unclear how money laundering patterns spanning separate bank graphs can be detected with federated learning.
method: The authors approximate remote account states locally using transactions already recorded by both endpoint banks, enabling multi-layer GNN computation without additional account-specific exchange, and test a disclosure ladder that shares either transaction counts or exact GNN states.
result: On AMLworld HI-Small across six GNN backbones and up to 32 silos, the observable baseline gives the largest gain, transaction counts provide a robust correction, and exact remote states help only in specific regimes; noise needed to protect shared states erases their detection value.
conclusion: The practical rule is for banks to use information they already record and formally protect only the small amount of information that must move between institutions.

title: Busta: Teaching Small Language Models To Reason About Binary Execution
authors: Ritika Poddar, Aidan Fennelly, Deirdre Murphy, Eric Wolos, Corre L. Steele, Michael Doyle
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLM) are increasingly applied to Reverse Engineering (RE) workflows. RE, however, differs from common LLM coding tasks as it requires models to reason about low-level program behavior. Furthermore, the deployment of tooling in resource-constrained sandboxed RE environments limits the ability to use frontier-scale solutions. We examine whether a targeted LLM training approach can transfer distinct RE skills to open models via inverse basic-block execution: given an x86-64 basic block and a desired output register state, the model predicts the input register values that produce it. Fine-tuning and with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) raises knowable-register prediction accuracy from 73.2\% to 85.3\% and from 63.3\% to 95.2\%, respectively. Frontier models still score highest (up to 99.2\%), but our fine-tuned comes within four points at a fraction of the parameter count. We release both fine-tuned models and the training dataset.
tldr: Busta fine-tunes and GRPO-trains small open language models to perform inverse basic-block execution on x86-64 code, predicting input register values from a desired output state.
motivation: Reverse engineering requires reasoning about low-level program behavior, but frontier LLMs are impractical in resource-constrained sandboxed RE environments, motivating targeted training of smaller open models.
method: The authors construct a dataset of x86-64 basic blocks and train open models via supervised fine-tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on the inverse basic-block execution task.
result: Fine-tuning raises knowable-register prediction accuracy from 73.2% to 85.3%, and GRPO from 63.3% to 95.2%, coming within four points of frontier models (up to 99.2%) at a fraction of the parameter count.
conclusion: Targeted training can transfer distinct reverse-engineering skills to small models, and the authors release the fine-tuned models and training dataset.

title: How Learning Selects Equilibria And When It Leads To Collusion
authors: Manxi Wu Hanzhang Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36306v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how learning algorithm design shapes equilibrium selection in infinite-horizon discounted Markov games with finite states and actions. Each episode, players choose smooth best responses to beliefs about opponents' policies, test them using noisy observations, and resample rejected beliefs or explore at rates determined by increasing transformations of their discounted values. We show that stochastically stable states induce approximate stationary Nash equilibria maximizing the minimum transformed discounted value across players, with transformations governing which players selection favors. In repeated games with bounded recall of noisy public signals, longer recall weakly increases the selected minimum transformed value. In repeated Cournot games, every stochastically stable state induces an approximate public perfect equilibrium whose minimum discounted profit across firms exceeds the Cournot-Nash benchmark. Collusion is therefore inevitable under these conditions and learning dynamics. For symmetric firms, selected profits can approach the monopoly benchmark arbitrarily closely. These results offer a novel equilibrium-selection perspective on algorithmic collusion.
tldr: The paper shows how the design of learning algorithms in infinite-horizon discounted Markov games selects stochastically stable states that induce approximate stationary Nash equilibria, and that in repeated Cournot games this leads to inevitable algorithmic collusion.
motivation: Algorithmic pricing agents raise worries of tacit collusion; the authors want a general equilibrium-selection account of when and why learning dynamics favor collusive outcomes.
method: Players play smooth best responses to beliefs about opponents, test them with noisy observations, and resample rejected beliefs or explore at rates set by increasing transformations of discounted values; stochastic-stability analysis of the resulting Markov process yields the selected states.
result: Stochastically stable states are approximate stationary Nash equilibria maximizing the minimum transformed discounted value, longer public-signal recall weakly increases this value, and in repeated Cournot games selected states are approximate public perfect equilibria beating the Cournot-Nash benchmark, approaching monopoly profit for symmetric firms.
conclusion: Under these learning conditions collusion is inevitable, offering an equilibrium-selection perspective on algorithmic collusion.

title: Reasoning About The Genetic Code In Lean
authors: Tyler R. Josephson Colin T. Jones
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36343v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The genetic code exhibits redundancy, meaning that multiple distinct nucleotide sequences can encode the same amino acid sequence, a property mathematically characterized as non-injectivity. While this phenomenon is well studied in molecular biology, its rigorous verification within a computational framework remains limited. In this work, we present a machine-verified model of the central dogma of molecular biology using the Lean 4 interactive theorem prover. We formalize nucleic acid bases and amino acids as inductive types and define transcription and translation as functions mapping DNA sequences to RNA and subsequently to polypeptides. Within this framework, we prove key properties of these biological processes, including the redundancy of the genetic code, injectivity of transcription, and the non-injectivity of translation. Additionally, we formalize auxiliary processes such as DNA replication and mutation, and verify properties such as length conservation under transcription and point mutations. Finally, we demonstrate how Lean 4 helps prevent semantic errors in our code, showing its effectiveness as a tool for advancing reliable, bug-free scientific computing, particularly within the life sciences.
tldr: The authors build a machine-verified Lean 4 model of the central dogma of molecular biology, proving properties such as the redundancy (non-injectivity) of the genetic code and the injectivity of transcription.
motivation: The redundancy of the genetic code is well studied in molecular biology, but rigorous computational verification of the central dogma's properties has been limited, motivating a formal, proof-checked treatment.
method: Nucleic acid bases and amino acids are encoded as inductive types in Lean 4, and transcription and translation are defined as functions on sequences, allowing formal proofs of their properties; DNA replication and mutation are also formalized.
result: The work yields formal proofs of genetic-code redundancy, injectivity of transcription, non-injectivity of translation, and length conservation under transcription and point mutations.
conclusion: Lean 4 is shown to be an effective tool for catching semantic errors and advancing reliable scientific computing in the life sciences.

title: Upper And Lower Bounds On The Complexity Of Unit-Distance Graph Realization In $\mathbb{Z}^d$
authors: Eric Binnendyk
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36516v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is known that the problem of recognizing the existence of a unit-distance realization in [MATH] for a graph [MATH] is NP-complete. Here, assuming ETH, we give a sub-exponential lower bound of [MATH] for this problem in [MATH] and [MATH] in [MATH], and give an upper bound of [MATH] for the time complexity with an explicit divide-and-conquer algorithm. This approach beats naive exhaustive search by a factor of [MATH] in the exponent. For 2 and 3 dimensions, our upper and lower bounds match to within a logarithmic factor.
tldr: The paper establishes conditional (ETH-based) sub-exponential lower bounds and matching divide-and-conquer upper bounds for deciding whether a graph admits a unit-distance realization in Z^d.
motivation: Recognizing unit-distance realizations of graphs is known to be NP-complete, but the fine-grained complexity of the problem as a function of dimension and graph size was not pinned down.
method: Fine-grained complexity analysis: reductions from SAT under the Exponential Time Hypothesis to obtain lower bounds, plus an explicit divide-and-conquer algorithm to obtain upper bounds, with exact matching up to logarithmic factors in d = 2, 3.
result: Sub-exponential lower bounds are given for d = 2 and d = 3 (and general d), together with an upper bound beating naive exhaustive search by a factor in the exponent; bounds match up to a log factor for two and three dimensions.
conclusion: The complexity of unit-distance graph realization in Z^d is characterized near-tightly for low dimensions, sharpening the picture beyond NP-completeness.

title: A Fibrational Framework For Multi-Conclusion Logics
authors: Oualid Merzouga
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The fibrational framework of Licata, Shulman, and Riley gives a uniform account of substructural and modal logics for single-conclusion judgments. This thesis extends it to a multiple-output setting in which cartesian resources may be used freely, while linear resources occur exactly once on either side of the turnstile. Judgments are indexed by descriptors: directed acyclic graphs generalizing the tree-shaped expressions of the original framework. Descriptor [MATH]-cells encode structural transformations, and explicit gates provide weakening, contraction, coweakening, and cocontraction at linear modes. We define a sequent calculus generated by two connectives, [MATH] and [MATH]. We prove identity, invertibility, and cut admissibility. The mode and type theories present linear-non-linear [MATH]-polycategories, and the projection is a local discrete fibration and a fibration, with opcartesian lifts for one-output base morphisms. Two adequacy results validate the framework: its cartesian fragment recovers the Licata--Shulman--Riley calculus, and its purely linear fragment presents classical multiplicative linear logic. Finally, we relate indexed and fibrational semantics. After developing representability correspondences for multicategories and polycategories, we establish an equivalence between multi-indexed categories over a fixed representable base and multicategorical opfibrations over it, together with its biclosed bifibrational version. We also give a one-way construction from planar poly-indexed data to a planar polycategory.
tldr: This thesis extends the fibrational framework of Licata, Shulman, and Riley to multi-conclusion (multiple-output) substructural and modal logics, presenting them as linear-non-linear polycategories.
motivation: The original fibrational framework only handles single-conclusion judgments, leaving multi-conclusion sequent calculi and their categorical semantics without a uniform account; the author aims to fill this gap.
method: Judgments are indexed by descriptor DAGs generalizing tree-shaped expressions, with descriptor cells encoding structural transformations and explicit gates for weakening, contraction, coweakening, and cocontraction at linear modes; a sequent calculus with two connectives is defined and shown to be a local discrete fibration.
result: Identity, invertibility, and cut admissibility are proved; adequacy results show the cartesian fragment recovers the Licata-Shulman-Riley calculus and the purely linear fragment presents classical multiplicative linear logic, plus an equivalence between multi-indexed categories over a representable base and multicategorical opfibrations.
conclusion: The work provides a coherent fibrational semantics for multi-conclusion logics and categorical structures such as polycategories, but lies entirely within pure categorical logic and proof theory.

title: Tight Characterizations Of Amm Mechanism Design Under Weak Efficiency
authors: Chengkai Zhang, Lirong Xia, Elaine Shi, Mengqian Zhang, Qishen Han, Yuhao Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36635v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Miner extractable value (MEV) poses a persistent challenge for blockchain ecosystems. It arises from the fact that a block builder can exploit its unilateral control over transaction inclusion and ordering to extract profit, potentially at users' expense. Recent work has explored consensus-aided mechanism design to mitigate MEV. This approach combines generic consensus-layer guarantees with application-layer mechanisms that use these guarantees to address application-specific MEV problems. Prior work exemplifies this approach for automated market makers (AMMs). When the consensus layer offers fair sequencing, which orders transactions according to their arrival times, their proposed mechanism achieves incentive compatibility (IC) and weak local efficiency (wLE). Informally, IC rules out profitable strategic deviations by users and builders. Meanwhile, wLE ensures that after execution, any order willing to trade at the initial price cannot benefit from further trade with the pool at the ending marginal price. In this work, we resolve the main open question left by prior works: whether IC and wLE can be achieved under plain consensus (e.g., current Ethereum) without fair sequencing. We prove that no deterministic, anonymous batch AMM can achieve both properties. The impossibility holds even when the consensus layer guarantees censorship resilience and block space is unlimited, establishing the first separation between censorship resilience and fair sequencing in the context of decentralized mechanism design. Our impossibility proof combines three strategic capabilities: creating Sybil identities, over-reporting budgets, and misreporting values. We further show the tightness of our impossibility result: removing any one from the strategy space restores feasibility under censorship resilience. Specifically, we construct a mechanism achieving IC and wLE for each restricted setting.
tldr: The paper proves an impossibility result showing that no deterministic anonymous batch AMM can simultaneously achieve incentive compatibility and weak local efficiency under plain consensus, and shows the result is tight by constructing mechanisms for restricted strategy spaces.
motivation: Miner extractable value (MEV) is a persistent problem in blockchains; prior consensus-aided AMM designs achieved IC and weak local efficiency only when the consensus layer provides fair sequencing, leaving open whether plain consensus suffices.
method: Formal mechanism-design analysis combining three adversarial capabilities (Sybil identities, budget over-reporting, value misreporting) to derive an impossibility theorem, plus constructive mechanisms for each relaxed setting.
result: A deterministic, anonymous batch AMM cannot achieve both IC and wLE even with censorship resilience and unlimited block space, establishing a separation between censorship resilience and fair sequencing; removing any single adversarial capability restores feasibility.
conclusion: Fair sequencing is strictly stronger than censorship resilience for MEV-resistant AMM design, and the impossibility is tight with respect to the assumed strategy space.

title: PrivacyEvalClaw: A Tool-Augmented Deliberative Agent For Auditing Privacy Leakage In Llm Jailbreak Responses
authors: Krishna Kanth Nakka, Yujun Wang, Shijie Zhou, Tu Nguyen, Gabriele Gelardi, Xuebing Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable evaluation is a critical bottleneck in privacy red-teaming of large language models (LLMs): determining whether a jailbreak response actually reveals personal information can be difficult when disclosures are indirect, contextual, partial, or obfuscated. Existing evaluation approaches increasingly rely on guard models and LLM-as-Judges, yet these evaluators may interpret the same response differently. To better characterize this evaluation setting, we conduct a systematic study of privacy evaluators and find substantial disagreement, particularly in ambiguous cases that require additional evidence or targeted analysis to resolve. Motivated by these findings, we introduce , a training-free deliberative agent for evaluating privacy leakage in LLM jailbreak responses. Rather than relying on isolated single-pass judgments, PrivacyEvalClaw treats evaluators and analysis modules as tools, adaptively gathers evidence, investigates uncertain disclosures, and reconciles conflicting signals before producing a final judgment. Our primary experiments use pairwise LLM-as-Judge evaluation of complete trajectories, showing that PrivacyEvalClaw achieves favorable win rates against competing baselines across outcome, process, and overall quality, while producing explicit reasoning traces that make the evaluation process more transparent and auditable.
tldr: PrivacyEvalClaw is a training-free deliberative LLM-agent framework for auditing privacy leakage in jailbreak responses by coordinating evaluator and analysis tools.
motivation: Privacy red-teaming of LLMs lacks reliable evaluation because guard models and LLM-as-judge evaluators disagree, especially for indirect, contextual, partial, or obfuscated disclosures.
method: The authors study evaluator disagreement and introduce a deliberative agent that treats evaluators and analysis modules as tools, adaptively gathers evidence, investigates uncertain disclosures, and reconciles conflicting signals before judging.
result: Using pairwise LLM-as-judge evaluation of complete trajectories, PrivacyEvalClaw achieves favorable win rates over baselines on outcome, process, and overall quality while producing transparent reasoning traces.
conclusion: The work improves LLM privacy-leakage auditing through tool-augmented deliberation, but it is unrelated to quantum information theory, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Balanced Active Subspaces For Optimal Control Via Trajectory Optimization
authors: Samuel E. Otto Emmanuel S. Ameh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The curse of dimensionality associated with solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation for the value function remains a key obstacle for real-time optimal feedback control of high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems. This is especially severe in aerospace applications such as relaminarizing unsteady turbulent flows and recovering from aerodynamic stall where nonlinear dynamics play a significant role. We introduce Balanced Active Subspaces for Optimal Control (BASOC), a model reduction framework which seeks to find directions in state space along which the value function is most sensitive, and the distribution of states exhibits maximum variance along optimal trajectories. BASOC leverages trajectory optimization and the Pontryagin minimum principle to obtain state and co-state (value function gradient) data along locally optimal trajectories for constructing state and gradient covariance matrices. Balancing these matrices provides an oblique projection for approximating the value function, which can also be used to construct reduced-order models and surrogate feedback control laws. We show that for linear-quadratic optimal control problems, BASOC becomes equivalent to a snapshot method for initial condition balancing of the optimally controlled closed-loop realization. The framework is demonstrated on a nonlinear three-dimensional system where POD and balanced truncation are known to perform poorly, and on the nonlinear complex Ginzburg-Landau equation to demonstrate feasibility for larger-scale systems.
tldr: BASOC is a model-reduction framework for high-dimensional nonlinear optimal feedback control that identifies state-space directions most relevant to the value function.
motivation: Solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation suffers from the curse of dimensionality, especially in aerospace control problems involving turbulent flows and stall recovery.
method: The authors use trajectory optimization and the Pontryagin minimum principle to collect state and co-state data, then balance state and gradient covariance matrices to construct an oblique projection for value-function approximation.
result: BASOC is shown to reduce to a snapshot balancing method for linear-quadratic problems and is demonstrated on a nonlinear three-dimensional system and the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation.
conclusion: The framework provides a promising reduced-order modeling and surrogate feedback control approach for high-dimensional nonlinear optimal control, but it has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Privately Clipping Heavy-Tailed Data
authors: Alex Kulesza Matthew Joseph
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36281v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Summing vectors is a basic task in differentially private data analysis. Standard private sum algorithms clip vectors to some bound, sum them, and add noise scaled to the bound. The differential privacy literature has developed a deep library of noise addition mechanisms, but it offers few tools for privately choosing a clipping bound based on the data. We introduce a method that privately chooses a clipping bound by optimizing residual coherence, the directional alignment of vectors exceeding the bound, against the variance cost of additional noise. We prove a close relationship between residual coherence and bias for a general class of heavy-tailed data regimes and show empirically that, across several datasets, our method outperforms existing baselines.
tldr: The paper introduces a differentially private method for choosing clipping bounds when summing heavy-tailed vectors by optimizing residual coherence against noise variance.
motivation: Private vector summation typically requires clipping to a fixed bound, but existing differential privacy tools provide limited guidance for privately selecting that bound from data.
method: The authors define residual coherence as the directional alignment of vectors exceeding the clipping bound and optimize it against the variance cost of added noise to privately choose the bound.
result: They prove a close relationship between residual coherence and bias for a broad class of heavy-tailed data regimes and empirically show improved performance over existing baselines across several datasets.
conclusion: The proposed coherence-based clipping method offers a principled and practical approach for private heavy-tailed vector summation, though it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: QMOMKit: A C++ Library For Quadrature-based Moment Methods
authors: Fabian Denner, Bruna Campos, Bruno Blais
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36189v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: QMOMKit is an open-source C++ library for the phase-space evolution of population balance equations with quadrature-based moment methods. The present version implements the quadrature method of moments (QMOM) and the conditional quadrature method of moments (CQMOM). QMOMKit is designed to be independent of any particular application and can be used either as a standalone solver for spatially homogeneous population models or as a local phase-space solver coupled to a host application. It handles the numerical aspects of the evolution of a population in phase space, including quadrature reconstruction, advection of the quadrature abscissas, and changes to the population through moment sources and phase-space boundary contributions. The number of quadrature nodes is adapted to what the supplied moments support, subject to prescribed bounds of the phase-space coordinates, and the CQMOM implementation supports an arbitrary number of phase-space dimensions as well as any conditioning order. The principal numerical algorithms of QMOMKit are verified against analytical and manufactured solutions. Standalone spatially homogeneous applications, ranging from aerosol evaporation to particle dynamics and fragmentation, are compared with Monte Carlo solutions of the same population models, while coupling examples with OpenFOAM and deal.II demonstrate how QMOMKit can be embedded in finite-volume and discontinuous-Galerkin simulation frameworks. Together, these capabilities provide a tested and reusable foundation for a wide range of population-balance problems, and a basis for extending QMOMKit to other quadrature-based moment methods.
tldr: QMOMKit is an open-source C++ library implementing quadrature-based moment methods (QMOM/CQMOM) for numerically evolving population balance equations in phase space.
motivation: Population balance models describing aerosol evaporation, particle dynamics, and fragmentation require robust, reusable numerical solvers for moment evolution, which are often re-implemented ad hoc in application codes.
method: The library implements quadrature method of moments and conditional quadrature method of moments, handling quadrature reconstruction, abscissa advection, moment sources, and phase-space boundary contributions, with adaptive node counts and support for arbitrary phase-space dimensions and conditioning order.
result: Core algorithms were verified against analytical and manufactured solutions, and standalone cases (aerosol evaporation, particle dynamics, fragmentation) matched Monte Carlo reference solutions; coupling examples with OpenFOAM and deal.II demonstrate embedding in finite-volume and discontinuous-Galerkin frameworks.
conclusion: QMOMKit provides a tested, reusable foundation for population-balance problems and a basis for extending to other quadrature-based moment methods.

title: There Are Exactly $2^\mathfrak{c}$ Simultaneously Bireflective And Bicoreflective Subconstructs Of $\mathbf{FTS}$
authors: Gao Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.35876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that there are exactly [MATH] simultaneously bireflective and bicoreflective subconstructs of [MATH]. By the Lowen--Wuyts bijection, these correspond to the total fuzzy topologies contained in [MATH], the fuzzy topology consisting of all nondecreasing left-continuous self-maps of the unit interval. The upper bound follows from a cardinality estimate. The matching lower bound is obtained by encoding [MATH] ultrafilters on [MATH] into total fuzzy topologies contained in [MATH].
tldr: The paper classifies all simultaneously bireflective and bicoreflective subconstructs of the category of fuzzy topological spaces, showing there are exactly 2^c many, corresponding via the Lowen–Wuyts bijection to total fuzzy topologies below the fuzzy topology of all nondecreasing left-continuous self-maps of [0,1].
motivation: The authors aim to fully determine the lattice of bireflective-and-bicoreflective subconstructs of FTS, a natural structural question in categorical fuzzy topology, and to identify them with a concrete class of total fuzzy topologies.
method: A cardinality estimate supplies the upper bound, while the lower bound is obtained by encoding ultrafilters on a set into total fuzzy topologies contained in the standard fuzzy topology of nondecreasing left-continuous self-maps of the unit interval.
result: Exactly 2^c such subconstructs exist, matching the cardinality of the set of ultrafilters used in the encoding construction.
conclusion: The classification is complete and sharp, establishing a bijective correspondence between these subconstructs and a specific family of total fuzzy topologies, with cardinality 2^c attained on both sides.

title: Soft Normed Linear Spaces Via Soft Elements: Decomposition, Convergence, And Operators
authors: Subhasis Ray
abstract: ArXiv:2610.35879v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a soft linear subspace of a linear space [MATH] over [MATH]. Its soft elements form the product [MATH]. We use this representation to characterize selection spaces, decompose soft norms and soft linear operators into their sectionwise parts, and compare soft, uniform, and componentwise convergence. We also characterize completeness and continuity in the box, extended-supremum, and product settings. Neumann-series and fixed-point results are obtained as applications.
tldr: This paper develops a mathematical theory of soft normed linear spaces via soft elements, including decomposition, convergence, completeness, continuity, and operator applications.
motivation: The work aims to characterize selection spaces and decompose soft norms and soft linear operators sectionwise within the framework of soft linear spaces.
method: It represents soft elements as a product space and compares soft, uniform, and componentwise convergence in box, extended-supremum, and product settings.
result: The paper establishes characterizations of completeness and continuity for soft normed linear spaces and derives Neumann-series and fixed-point results as applications.
conclusion: The results contribute to abstract soft functional analysis but have no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Counterexample To A Bourgain-Brezis Sum-Space Estimate
authors: Chenye Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.35882v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A question of Bourgain and Brezis, later restated as Open Problem 7.1 by Brezis, asks whether the [MATH] norm of a mean-zero scalar function is controlled by the ambient [MATH] sum norm of its gradient. We show that this estimate fails in every dimension [MATH]. More precisely, for every integer [MATH], we construct a smooth real-valued mean-zero function [MATH] on [MATH] such that [MATH] and [MATH], where the absolute constants [MATH] are independent of [MATH] and [MATH]. Equivalently, the ratio of the gradient-constrained decomposition cost to the ambient decomposition cost is unbounded. The construction applies the Hodge projection to a smooth approximation of a normal vector measure on a codimension-one sheet. Its potential records lacunary partial sums at geometrically separated distances from the sheet. A scale-path lower bound, combined with an odd critical Hardy inequality, excludes uniformly bounded [MATH] decompositions.
tldr: The paper disproves a conjectured Bourgain-Brezis sum-space estimate by constructing smooth mean-zero counterexamples in every dimension.
motivation: Brezis restated as Open Problem 7.1 the question of whether the L^1 norm of a mean-zero scalar function is controlled by the L^1 sum norm of its gradient; this work answers it negatively.
method: For each dimension the author applies a Hodge projection to a smooth approximation of a normal vector measure supported on a codimension-one sheet, with a potential recording lacunary partial sums, and proves a scale-path lower bound using an odd critical Hardy inequality.
result: For every integer dimension a smooth real-valued mean-zero function is constructed whose gradient decomposition cost is unbounded relative to the ambient decomposition cost, showing the estimate fails in all dimensions.
conclusion: The Bourgain-Brezis sum-space estimate is false in every dimension, settling the open problem negatively via a geometric measure-theoretic construction.

title: On Baireness Of The Wijsman Topology
authors: Basile Beyer de Ryke
abstract: ArXiv:2610.35921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give negative answers to Questions 4.4 and 4.5 in Cao's survey on the Wijsman topology. We construct a metrizable space [MATH] and a compatible metric [MATH] such that every finite power [MATH] is Baire, while [MATH] is not Baire. The construction realizes the Vietoris hyperspace of a suitable metric space as an open subspace of a ball hyperspace. We also study the set [MATH] of points having an open [MATH]-[MATH]-totally bounded neighborhood. We prove that Baireness of [MATH] implies Baireness of [MATH], and that, whenever [MATH] is dense in [MATH], the following three conditions are equivalent: [MATH] is Baire, [MATH] is Baire, and [MATH] is Baire. As consequences, we obtain complete characterizations for locally [MATH]-[MATH]-totally bounded metric spaces, countable metric spaces, and [MATH]-compact metrizable spaces. In our counterexample, [MATH] coincides with a non-dense discrete component for every compatible metric [MATH], showing that the density assumption is essential.
tldr: This paper resolves two open questions in Cao's survey on the Wijsman topology by constructing a metrizable space whose finite powers are all Baire while the hyperspace itself is not.
motivation: The Wijsman topology on hyperspaces has open questions about when Baireness of finite powers transfers to the hyperspace, and the authors aim to settle Questions 4.4 and 4.5 from Cao's survey.
method: The authors construct a compatible metric on a metrizable space, realizing the Vietoris hyperspace of a suitable metric space as an open subspace of a ball hyperspace, and analyze the set of points admitting an open totally bounded neighborhood.
result: They show Baireness of a set implies Baireness of the hyperspace, prove equivalences under density assumptions, and give complete characterizations for locally totally bounded, countable, and compact metrizable spaces, plus a counterexample showing the density assumption is essential.
conclusion: Baireness of finite powers does not imply Baireness of the Wijsman hyperspace, answering Cao's questions negatively and settling the role of density assumptions.

title: Setting Things Straight: On The Straightness And Non-Straightness Of Two-Step Rectified Flow
authors: Tuan Pham, Saptarshi Roy, Alessandro Rinaldo, Purnamrita Sarkar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rectified flow (RF) is an ODE-based generative modeling framework that has achieved remarkable success in practice over the past few years. By design, RF seeks to produce flows that have a high degree of straightness, in the sense that the resulting ODE trajectories can be obtained with relatively few (ideally, one) sampling steps. However, a rigorous analysis of straightness or near-straightness of RF flows remains missing in the literature. In this paper, we study settings in which the coupling generated by two-step RF is provably straight at the population level. We provide a complete characterization in two popular classes of data distributions: (i) smooth, strongly log-concave densities and (ii) Gaussian mixture models. Our main results yield sharp conditions for the coupling generated by two-step RF to be straight. Non-straight couplings are constructed when these conditions fail, which demonstrate the sharpness of these conditions. Using the theory developed on the straightness of two-step RF, we propose a notion of approximate straightness that measures the straightness of the learned couplings and can be estimated from the data. We describe a procedure for constructing asymptotic confidence intervals for our proposed notion of approximate straightness and propose a data-driven method for selecting the number of reflow rounds in multiple iterations of RF.
tldr: This paper rigorously characterizes when the coupling produced by two-step rectified flow is exactly straight at the population level, for strongly log-concave densities and Gaussian mixture models, and proposes an estimable notion of approximate straightness.
motivation: Rectified flow is designed to yield nearly straight ODE trajectories so that few sampling steps suffice, but no rigorous theory of straightness or near-straightness existed.
method: The authors derive sharp necessary and sufficient conditions for straightness of two-step RF couplings in two distribution classes, construct counterexamples showing sharpness, and develop a data-estimable approximate-straightness measure with asymptotic confidence intervals and a reflow-round selection procedure.
result: Complete characterizations of provable straightness are obtained for smooth strongly log-concave densities and Gaussian mixtures, with explicit non-straight counterexamples when the conditions fail.
conclusion: The theory clarifies when rectified flow can be sampled in one or few steps and provides practical, data-driven tools for assessing straightness and choosing the number of reflow iterations.

title: Computer-assisted Proofs Of Periodic Solutions Of State-dependent Delay Equations Beyond Perturbative Regimes
authors: Jan Bouwe van Den Berg, Maxime Breden, Matthieu Cadiot, Kevin E. M. Church, Jean-Philippe Lessard
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rigorous existence results for periodic solutions of state-dependent delay differential equations (SDDEs) are scarce outside perturbative regimes, where the equation is close to an ordinary or constant-delay differential equation. We develop a computer-assisted framework that proves the existence of periodic solutions of SDDEs directly. The numerical approximation is a trigonometric polynomial, and a true periodic solution nearby is obtained by a Newton--Kantorovich argument in the space of [MATH] periodic functions. The main difficulty lies in the terms in which the solution is evaluated at a time that itself depends on the solution. We obtain rigorous enclosures of their Fourier coefficients by adapting validated discrete Fourier transform techniques for analytic nonlinearities. We apply the framework to three representative examples of increasing complexity: a periodically forced toy model, an autonomous scalar equation with two state-dependent delays, and a threshold-type delay model from operon dynamics in gene regulation. To our knowledge, these are the first computer-assisted proofs of existence of periodic solutions of SDDEs outside perturbative regimes. This opens the way to computer-assisted proofs for SDDEs more broadly. All computer-assisted proofs, including the requisite codes and the approximate objects, are accessible on GitHub at .
tldr: The paper develops a computer-assisted framework using Newton–Kantorovich arguments and validated discrete Fourier transform techniques to rigorously prove the existence of periodic solutions of state-dependent delay differential equations (SDDEs) outside perturbative regimes.
motivation: Rigorous existence results for periodic solutions of SDDEs are scarce except near ordinary or constant-delay limits, so a direct validated approach is needed.
method: The numerical approximation is a trigonometric polynomial, and a genuine periodic solution nearby is proven via a Newton–Kantorovich argument in the space of periodic functions, using rigorous enclosure of Fourier coefficients for solution-dependent evaluation times.
result: The framework is applied to three examples of increasing complexity — a periodically forced toy model, an autonomous scalar equation with two state-dependent delays, and a threshold-type delay model from operon gene regulation — yielding the first computer-assisted existence proofs beyond perturbative regimes.
conclusion: The work opens the way toward broader computer-assisted proofs for SDDEs, with all proofs and code publicly available.

title: A Unified Family Of Multiblock Admm Schemes By Means Of Graph Splitting
authors: Rub\'en Campoy, Scott B. Lindstrom, C\'esar L\'opez-Pastor
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces a novel unified family of multiblock ADMM schemes by combining Gabay duality with a graph-based splitting methodology. This framework allows us to recover existing ADMM algorithms as particular instances, as well as to generate new ones by varying the underlying network topology. We focus specifically on the case of the complete graph, a structure of significant practical interest due to its dense connectivity, for which we provide a fully explicit and directly implementable scheme. We further derive an equivalent reformulation of the proposed family in which the algorithm is expressed in terms of a reduced set of dual variables, which clarifies its connection to the classical ADMM framework. Numerical experiments are conducted to compare the performance of different graph choices, showing particularly favorable results for the complete graph.
tldr: The paper introduces a unified family of multiblock ADMM splitting schemes derived from Gabay duality and graph-based splitting, with an explicit complete-graph variant validated numerically.
motivation: Multiblock ADMM lacks a unifying framework; the authors aim to systematize existing schemes and generate new ones by varying the underlying graph topology.
method: They combine Gabay duality with graph splitting to define a family of algorithms, derive a reduced dual-variable reformulation linking back to classical ADMM, and specialize to the complete graph for an explicit implementable scheme.
result: Existing ADMM algorithms are recovered as special cases, new schemes arise from different graph choices, and numerical experiments show favorable performance for the complete-graph variant.
conclusion: Graph topology provides a useful design axis for multiblock ADMM, with the complete graph being practically attractive.

title: Hidden Convexity In Multi-Retailer Cold-Chain Allocation: A Cholesky-Spectral Second-Order Cone Programming Approach
authors: Thinh Nguyen Hoang Pham, Boris Mordukhovich, Son Hoang Truong, Ngoc Anh Tran, Quyen Phuong Le
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36350v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Several dairy retailers share a refrigerated cold-chain network, each allocating products across heat-sensitivity subgroups to maximize quadratic-fractional efficiency (DEA style). This formulation measures spoilage risk per unit of logistics cost, separating technical from scale efficiency. The single-agent problem is a non-convex fractional QCQP, while the multi-retailer game forms a generalized Nash equilibrium problem (GNEP) with a shared risk-budget constraint, which is generally NP-hard. Governed by the Arrhenius spoilage law, the thermal-risk covariance inherits a rank-one-plus-diagonal structure that unlocks hidden convexity. The authors propose the HSDI (Hidden SOCP Dinkelbach Iteration) algorithm via a joint Cholesky-spectral transform. Key contributions include: 1. Establishing simultaneous diagonalization of without requiring matrix commutativity. 2. Deriving an explicit sufficient condition for exact second-order cone programming (SOCP) relaxation, alongside a closed-form suboptimality bound for inexact regimes. 3. Proving global convergence: the outer Dinkelbach loop converges Q-superlinearly (exact) or R-linearly (inexact), and the coupled variational-equilibrium (VE) iteration converges R-linearly under strong monotonicity, achieving an overall complexity while ensuring Lipschitz stability of the primal-dual pair. Calibrated on Vietnam and US dairy markets, HSDI matches the objective value of multi-start non-linear baselines without random restarts, yielding global optima under exactness. HSDI exhibits an empirical scaling exponent of 0.93 (versus 1.30 for SLSQP), offering a certified polynomial-time framework and a stable shadow price for prioritizing cold-chain investments.
tldr: The paper develops a Cholesky-spectral second-order cone programming algorithm (HSDI) for multi-retailer cold-chain product allocation, exploiting hidden convexity in a rank-one-plus-diagonal thermal-risk covariance structure to solve a generalized Nash equilibrium problem with shared risk budget.
motivation: Dairy retailers sharing a refrigerated cold-chain network need to allocate heat-sensitive products to maximize DEA-style quadratic-fractional efficiency (spoilage risk per unit logistics cost), but the resulting multi-agent problem is a non-convex fractional QCQP game that is generally NP-hard.
method: The authors exploit the Arrhenius-law-induced rank-one-plus-diagonal structure of the thermal-risk covariance to derive a joint Cholesky-spectral transform, giving simultaneous diagonalization without commutativity, and embed it in a Dinkelbach iteration coupled with a variational-equilibrium iteration (HSDI) with an explicit SOCP exactness condition.
result: Global convergence is proved (Q-superlinear exact, R-linear inexact outer loop; R-linear coupled VE iteration) with polynomial complexity and Lipschitz stability of the primal-dual pair; on Vietnam and US dairy data HSDI matches multi-start nonlinear baselines without restarts and shows an empirical scaling exponent of 0.93 versus 1.30 for SLSQP.
conclusion: The work provides a certified polynomial-time framework for cold-chain allocation with stable shadow prices for investment prioritization, but it lies entirely in operations research and optimization rather than quantum information science.

title: Asynchronous Parallel Computation Of Lagrangian Bounds For Mixed-Integer Stochastic Programs By Frank-Wolfe Methods Within Projective Hedging
authors: Jonathan Eckstein, Jean-Paul Watson, David L. Woodruff
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36376v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We describe an asynchronous parallel method to calculate Lagrangian bounds for mixed-integer stochastic programming problems. As in some prior work, we use a fully corrective Frank-Wolfe method on subproblems within a decomposition method, eventually optimizing subproblems for individual scenarios over the convex hulls of their integer-feasible vertices. However, instead of using progressive hedging as our decomposition algorithm, we employ an asynchronous projective hedging method. Like our earlier work on projective hedging, our algorithm need only solve a subset of the scenario subproblems at each iteration. Here, we further exploit the capabilities of projective hedging to create a parallel implementation capable of fully asynchronous operation. As we demonstrate empirically, this capability can lead to significant efficiency improvements when the subproblems are solved by Frank-Wolfe and have highly variable solve times.
tldr: The paper presents an asynchronous parallel algorithm for computing Lagrangian bounds in mixed-integer stochastic programs using fully corrective Frank-Wolfe subproblem solves within an asynchronous projective hedging decomposition.
motivation: Solving large mixed-integer stochastic programs is computationally expensive, and existing decomposition approaches for Lagrangian bounds either require synchronized iterations or solve all scenario subproblems each round, limiting parallel efficiency when subproblem solve times vary widely.
method: The authors combine a fully corrective Frank-Wolfe method that optimizes each scenario subproblem over the convex hull of its integer-feasible vertices with an asynchronous projective hedging decomposition scheme, allowing only a subset of scenario subproblems to be solved per iteration and enabling fully asynchronous parallel execution.
result: Empirical experiments show that the fully asynchronous operation yields significant efficiency improvements over prior projective hedging approaches, particularly when the Frank-Wolfe subproblems exhibit highly variable solve times.
conclusion: Asynchronous projective hedging with Frank-Wolfe subproblem solves offers a scalable and efficient route to Lagrangian bounds for mixed-integer stochastic programs on parallel hardware.

title: Shape Optimization Under Minimal Width And Constant Width Constraints
authors: Beniamin Bogosel
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36382v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we study shape optimization problems for planar convex sets with prescribed minimal width or constant width. We prove that the Reuleaux triangle minimizes torsional rigidity among sets of constant width. We also show that the first Dirichlet-Laplace eigenvalue is maximized by the equilateral triangle under a minimal width constraint and by the Reuleaux triangle under a constant width constraint. The proofs use subsets consisting of a disk and three straight or circular caps. Reflection arguments reduce the study to equilateral configurations, which contain a polygon or a disk polygon depending on one parameter. The same cap constructions give a common proof of the known area, Cheeger and inner parallel area inequalities, and yield sharp bounds for all positive moments of the distance to the boundary. We also prove sharp inequalities for concentric disk intersections and decreasing radial integrals, and compare interaction energies for kernels close to a positive constant. This includes a nonempty interval of positive Riesz exponents. Finally, we investigate whether inclusion monotonicity and Minkowski concavity suffice to obtain these comparisons for other functionals.
tldr: The paper proves sharp geometric inequalities for planar convex sets under minimal-width and constant-width constraints, showing the Reuleaux triangle minimizes torsional rigidity and the equilateral triangle maximizes the first Dirichlet-Laplace eigenvalue under a minimal width constraint.
motivation: Shape optimization with width constraints is a classical geometric analysis problem whose extremal configurations (Reuleaux triangle, equilateral triangle) are of intrinsic mathematical interest and connect to known area, Cheeger, and inner parallel area inequalities.
method: The proofs construct comparison subsets made of a disk plus three straight or circular caps, use reflection arguments to reduce to equilateral configurations parameterized by one variable, and derive sharp bounds via these cap constructions and radial-integral comparisons.
result: Sharp inequalities are obtained for torsional rigidity, the first Dirichlet-Laplace eigenvalue, all positive moments of the distance to the boundary, concentric disk intersections, decreasing radial integrals, and interaction energies for kernels near a positive constant including a range of positive Riesz exponents.
conclusion: The unified cap-based framework recovers and extends several known geometric inequalities, and the authors discuss whether inclusion monotonicity and Minkowski concavity suffice to extend the comparisons to other functionals.

title: Log-To-Leak: Prompt Injection Attacks On Tool-Using Llm Agents Via The Model Context Protocol
authors: Yuepeng Hu, Chongyu Fan, Sirat Samyoun, Jian Du
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents increasingly access external tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), but the natural-language metadata used to describe those tools creates a prompt-injection surface. Within this established tool-poisoning surface, we study Log-To-Leak, an additive post-hoc logging attack that induces a separate attacker-controlled call after the final legitimate call. Its payload targets the user query, MCP server name, server response, and agent response. We operationalize the injected directive through Trigger, Tool Binding, Justification, and Pressure, and separately measure call success, payload fidelity, and preservation of legitimate behavior. We evaluate five MCP servers and four LLM agents using five metrics spanning effectiveness, utility, and efficiency. Across 18 model-server pairs with valid tool execution, Log-To-Leak achieves an attack success rate (ASR) of 62.64-100% and conditional logging accuracy (LA) of 76.55-95.64%; 16 pairs have absolute target-task completion changes of at most 6.63 percentage points. Three evaluated defenses leave residual ASR above 55% on GitHub MCP with GPT-4o, while an instruction detector flags 85.53% of benign descriptions. These results show that successful task completion can coexist with unauthorized post-hoc disclosure and motivate host-controlled authorization for secondary tool calls.
tldr: The paper introduces Log-To-Leak, a prompt-injection attack in which malicious natural-language tool metadata on MCP servers induces an LLM agent to make an extra attacker-controlled logging call after its legitimate task completes.
motivation: LLM agents increasingly reach external tools through the Model Context Protocol, and the natural-language metadata that describes those tools creates a prompt-injection surface that can enable unauthorized data disclosure even while the user's task is completed.
method: The authors design an additive post-hoc logging payload that targets the user query, server name, server response, and agent response, structured through Trigger, Tool Binding, Justification, and Pressure, and evaluate it across five MCP servers and four LLM agents using five metrics covering effectiveness, utility, and efficiency, along with three defenses.
result: On the 18 model-server pairs with valid tool execution, the attack reaches an ASR of 62.64-100% and conditional logging accuracy of 76.55-95.64%, while target-task completion changes by at most 6.63 percentage points in 16 pairs; three defenses leave residual ASR above 55% on GitHub MCP with GPT-4o even though an instruction detector flags 85.53% of benign descriptions.
conclusion: Successful task completion can coexist with covert post-hoc data disclosure, so host-controlled authorization for secondary tool calls is needed to mitigate this MCP tool-poisoning threat.

title: Detecting And Mitigating Query-Based System Prompt Leakage Attacks
authors: Tushar Nayan, Pratik Poudel, Qian Lou, Yuede Ji, Jason Liu, Ruimin Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on proprietary system prompts to enforce task directives, safety policies, and access controls. These prompts are vulnerable to query-based leakage attacks, where black-box adversaries extract confidential instructions through adaptive, multi-turn interactions. Existing defenses often assess queries independently, missing malicious behavior that emerges across interactions. We present AdvGuard, a model-agnostic framework for detecting and mitigating system prompt leakage. AdvGuard models cross-query relationships using a bounded semantic interaction graph, statistically filters candidate components, and converts them into line graphs for graph convolutional network (GCN) classification. This approach captures multi-hop patterns in query similarity that distinguish coordinated extraction from benign workflows. A lightweight prompt-level detector provides protection before sufficient interaction history accumulates, and the framework supports black-box LLM deployments. In mixed-query evaluations, AdvGuard improves recall by up to 36% over the strongest baseline while maintaining a false positive rate of at most 3.4%. In multi-turn workloads, it achieves 97.23%-99.1% F1 with 100% recall. Leave-one-attack-family-out tests yield 99.98% mean recall and 99.99% mean F1, with no observed false positives. Integrated into the adaptive PLeak and LeakAgent attack loops, AdvGuard limits exact-match leakage to 0.00-0.01 and substring-match leakage to 0.01-0.09 across evaluated victim models. These results demonstrate robust detection of unseen attack families and substantially reduced prompt reconstruction.
tldr: AdvGuard is a model-agnostic framework that detects and mitigates query-based system prompt leakage attacks against black-box LLMs by modeling cross-query relationships with a bounded semantic interaction graph and GCN classification.
motivation: Proprietary system prompts in LLMs encode task directives, safety policies, and access controls, but black-box adversaries can extract them through adaptive multi-turn querying; existing defenses evaluate queries independently and miss malicious patterns emerging across interactions.
method: The authors build a bounded semantic interaction graph over queries, statistically filter candidate components, convert them into line graphs, and classify with a graph convolutional network, supplemented by a lightweight prompt-level detector for early-stage protection.
result: AdvGuard improves recall by up to 36% over the strongest baseline at ≤3.4% false positive rate, reaches 97.23–99.1% F1 with 100% recall in multi-turn workloads, and limits exact-match leakage to 0.00–0.01 when integrated into adaptive PLeak/LeakAgent attack loops.
conclusion: Graph-based cross-query modeling enables robust detection of unseen attack families and substantially reduces prompt reconstruction in black-box LLM deployments.

title: What Victims Take Away: Attack Reuse And Defense Revision After Prompt-Injection Attacks
authors: Zihan Chen, Lei Nico Zheng, Di Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.36422v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attack logs and red-team reports show targets the attacks used against them, to help them repair their defenses. Prompt injections against large language models (LLMs) are plain text, so such records also hand targets a working copy. Drawing on social learning theory and work on the victim-offender overlap, we study what targets do with that copy in Tensor Trust, an online game whose players defended LLM-guarded accounts, attacked one another's, and could read every attack they received. Using all 563,349 attack records, we compare each received attack with matched attacks that circulated among similar players at the same moment but never reached the target. Reuse mainly followed success: within a week, targets attacked other players with 10.0% of the attacks that had broken their defense, versus 0.03% of matched attacks (adjusted difference: 8.8-10.0 percentage points). Near-misses, whose replies began with "access granted" but that scored as failures, were reused about as rarely as failures: reuse tracked whether an attack paid off, not how its reply read, consistent with payoff-biased social learning. Breaches were also followed by defense changes, after which same-family attacks became 24.5 percentage points less successful against the target, relative to other defenders. Reuse came mainly from players already attacking, not newcomers. Previously received texts accounted for 23.2% of the successful hijacks we analyze. The attack history thus served both repair and reuse; we derive testable hypotheses for how AI security tools should disclose attacks, such as describing the technique without the full text.
tldr: An empirical study of how defenders in an LLM prompt-injection game reuse attacks they received and revise their defenses afterward.
motivation: Attack logs and red-team reports are shared with victims to help them repair defenses, but because prompt injections are plain text, the same records hand victims a working exploit; the authors ask what targets actually do with that copy.
method: Using all 563,349 attack records from the online game Tensor Trust, each received attack is compared with matched attacks that circulated among similar players at the same time but never reached the target, and subsequent defense changes are tracked.
result: Reuse tracked success rather than appearance: 10.0% of successful attacks were reused within a week versus 0.03% of matched attacks, near-misses were reused as rarely as failures, and breaches were followed by defense changes that cut same-family attack success by 24.5 percentage points.
